Breaking.title: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land £36m mega donation
Breaking.text:
Look closely at the posters, placards and online posts. Your eyes aren't deceiving you if Labour's red seems a little deeper and the Conservatives' blue a little truer.

Politics seems to have found a new rhythm, one that feels a little familiar, despite Reform's jaw-dropping new donations putting it back in the headlines today.

For the avoidance of doubt, the scale of that initial £36m gift to Nigel Farage's party alone is like something from a different political universe.

"It's a gobsmacking sum," a senior figure involved in running successive election campaigns for one of the big parties tells me.

That was even before another Reform donor pledged to match that astonishing sum with another £36m, saying the first donation had provoked his "competitive spirit".

But one cabinet minister is enjoying what they see as a newly obvious difference between Labour and the Tories. "It's clarifying," they say, a clear gap between Labour and the Tories' "sense of purpose and values".

A member of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's top team tells me, "normal jogging is reasserting itself", hopeful they're at the start of a more straightforward, routine moment in politics after years of craziness, with smaller parties vying to shove the traditional tribes out of the way.

The standout moment was at the despatch box this week when Prime Minister Andy Burnham declared that national security couldn't come at the expense of social security - a phrase immediately seized on by the Tories, interpreting it as the PM saying he'd never cut welfare spending to pay for defence.

One senior conservative said: "It was a real line in the sand, we could never have imagined Sir Keir Starmer saying that."

The party seems cock-a-hoop at a line they can use again and again, asserting the prime minister cares more about welfare than guarding against war.

But there is a positive atmosphere in No 10 too, one source telling me that the face-offs between Badenoch and Burnham have "breathed new life into the Labour versus Tory dynamic".

How can they both be happy, when ultimately politics is a contest and there can only be one winner in the end?

Well, on the security spat, Burnham's backers are adamant he does want to cut welfare spending, and find more money for defence. How does that stack up with his words this week?

I'm told No 10 will explain in more detail his belief that security also means secure communities, which aren't created by slashing benefits.

Crucially, they reckon while cutting welfare might appeal to some voters, "once you dig into the 'who' and the 'how' of doing that, public support wavers, and when Kemi talks about housing benefit cuts, public opinion goes all over the shop".

They even cite that moment as evidence that the prime minister is "happy to grab thorny issues and put himself at the centre of them", as he did with the early release of prisoners.

He'll give a grabby-sounding view before the government has found a solution to a problem, stake part of his reputation on it, and make the case, hoping it will work out.

The choices are only going to get harder and harder though. "Hope" as a slogan and a strategy could never be enough.

But when politics is fundamentally a contest, how can both the traditional political tribes be buoyant?

For Labour, it's not just the obvious change of leader to a more effective politician who is much more at ease talking to the public, whether that's an eight-second TikTok or his long explanations of his positions expressed in a newspaper opinion piece and posted on Facebook.

It's that Burnham is making arguments that are more appealing to Labour's psychology – build council houses, take stronger action against the worst excesses of the Israeli government, stand up for those who need to rely on benefits from the state.

Labour believes, for now, they have a leader who is simply a better politician, who is making arguments many of them find instinctively more appealing.

The party knows what its leader believes, broadly at least. As one senior figure said: "He has a worldview which the last one didn't - he's clear what he wants and he's grabbed the reins of power."

Another who has worked under Starmer and now Burnham said: "It's just chalk and cheese."

And don't underestimate the importance of keeping backbenchers content, feeling understood. A government source joked the whips, the party managers, are becoming a bit "like an HR department" listening to concerns rather than driving the troops forward.

But as Starmer found to his cost, backbenchers weren't prepared to be loyal to him when many felt he hadn't shown much care or loyalty to them.

But Badenoch's tribe also seems more chipper because, as she has told friends, there is now a sharper ideological divide between the two parties saying, "it's much clearer to have those arguments rather than a process discussion with Starmer".

Shadow ministers reckon it's easier to make classic Conservative arguments because in the words of one, "Andy Burnham is a classic old leftie and we're the obvious answer to that".

Shock, horror, Labour sources I put that to dispute that is the case, one close ally calling him "a pragmatist", another denying he's further to the left than Starmer, because, "Keir was so hard to place".

But one conservative source also pointedly wonders how long Labour's happiness with their new leader will last, given Burnham's rapid return to Parliament saying, "looking at the benches opposite there is a vision of somebody who has turned up to a Tinder date and doesn't quite look like his profile pic".

Ouch.

Will this newly refreshed red-blue battle prove to be the real deal?

Rhetorical lines have been drawn this week, but real choices and arguments loom, and the bouncy feeling around the place may not last, especially when it comes to finding cash for the prime minister's big promises.

Downing Street sources acknowledge privately that bringing down the welfare bill in the way that Alan Milburn envisages, with his report expected, but not confirmed, to come before the Budget, will need billions spent up front, money the government might struggle to find.

Similarly, to build the council houses Burnham desires to cut the housing benefits bill will need big cheques.

It's one thing promising those Labour friendly dreams. It's another, perhaps at the party conference, to answer the much harder question of how the government plans to pay.

It won't be easy for a mid-term prime minister to find money in the short term that might only produce savings in the years to come.

But Burnham's Labour are happy to talk about the economy and how they want to help hard-up families, still citing the chaos of Liz Truss and keen to underline the early steps the prime minister has taken to ease the pressure.

With borrowing costs and the country's debt seriously sky high, the Conservatives are pleased to sketch out a classic left-right argument too.

It's also true they have both been enjoying the moment of real pressure on their opponents in Reform, who have slipped back in the polls, besieged by claims and counter claims about party funding.

Although this weekend's mega donations illustrate that Nigel Farage still has the capacity to bust political conventions, the money from the crypto billionaire, Ben Delo, and cryptocurrency investor, Christopher Harborne, is completely off the charts for our politics.

Talking about the initial donation, a senior figure told me: "To put £36 m in context, one man has donated a sum bigger than Labour's entire 2024 election budget, bigger than the Conservatives', and about six times what Reform actually spent.

"It's the kind of donation that could change how politics is funded in the UK."

During the last general election campaign Labour raised about £9m, the Tories, Reform and the Lib Dems all less than £2m.

These extra millions give Farage enormous and immediate spending power, and there might be more to come. Although you can bet the other parties will cry foul over the scale of this big money coming from men with deep pockets, not least because Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over violating the Bank Secrecy Act.

It would be daft for either of the two main parties to assume this apparent return to traditional two-party politics is here to stay. But it is strangely new to be in a moment when both Labour and the Conservatives are broadly content.

As the new prime minister's universe settles, a key Labour figure observed: "We've had the amuse–bouche and it was very tasty. What happens next?"

Breaking.title: Donald Trump: A united Ireland would be 'fantastic' says Trump during Irish visit
Breaking.text:
US President Donald Trump has said he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with the Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) during a visit in Dublin.

Trump is on a two-day visit to the country where earlier he had a courtesy call with the Irish President Catherine Connolly at the Áras an Uachtaráin - the official residence of the Irish president.

He attended meetings in Dublin, before travelling to County Clare for the Amgen Irish Open golf tournament.

Trump said a united Ireland would happen eventually and that the Taoiseach was "the right man over here to get it moving".

During his meeting with Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House, in Phoenix Park, Trump said a united Ireland would be a "fantastic thing", and added: "now the UK would have something to say about it obviously but I think it would be a great thing, I mean, how can it be bad?"

A spokesperson for Number 10 referred to Prime Minister Andy Burnham's words on Wednesday in the House of Commons that he "will stick to it (the Good Friday Agreement) 100%".

On Wednesday, Burnham added that "the question of a border poll" was for the Northern Ireland secretary "when there is clear consensus in the country - when public opinion has changed to the point at which the call has to be considered".

Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said she acknowledged Trumps comments on a united Ireland and said the onus is on the Taoiseach to begin planning.

"Our national journey is now reunification, which is organised, planned and a peaceful transition."

Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said Trump "knows better than most that elections matter".

"Northern Ireland's constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington," he said.

He added that Northern Ireland is part of the UK because it is the "settled democratic will of its people" and added he is confident the country will continue to choose the UK.

Former DUP MP Ian Paisley and close friend of the Trump family said: "everyone is allowed a personal opinion even when it's wrong".

Welcoming his comments, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) Claire Hanna said there was something "fairly extraordinary" about Trump standing in Dublin and talking openly about Irish unity.

"When even Donald Trump has clocked that Irish unity is no longer some distant or theoretical prospect, it tells you something about just how far this conversation has shifted."

The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows said while America is an "important ally," Northern Ireland's future will be decided by its people.

"That is the principle of consent, now enshrined in law through the Belfast Agreement."

The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said Trump "is not the first US President to meddle in the affairs which don't concern him".

"Northern Ireland not a pawn in Trump's fall out with the UK. Our constitutional future does not depend on him or any other foreign dignitary," Allister added.

Ireland's Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said: "Something to this magnitude can only happen where there's consent from the Irish people.

"It's something that that we have to work on and we have to work towards."

Later, while attending an event at the US Ambassador to Ireland's residence, Trump said there is "no good answer" to a question about a united Ireland.

Recalling the moment, he said: "Oh that's a nice question, I have a nice answer, I think, we'll read about it tomorrow."

Protesters have also gathered in Doonbeg, a few miles from Trump's hotel where he will attend the Irish Open.

He will be accompanied by his sons Eric and Donald Trump Junior.

There is a heavy Garda (Irish Police) presence, road closures and countless tricolour bunting through the village.

Sixty-year-old Jessie Phillips is in Doonbeg to protest

She lives in county Clare but is originally from Tennessee and said she was protesting as a "concerned member of the public".

"I just want him [President Trump] to see my placard so he knows I don't care for him and that my family doesn't care for him and that he's not welcome here or over there in my opinion."

Breaking.title: Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war
Breaking.text:
The Houthis' lightning advance across the southern reaches of the Tihamah – Yemen's arid coastal plain – appears to have taken most observers by surprise.

Until recently, the anti-Houthi coalition known as the National Resistance held significant territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast. In a matter of days, much of this has fallen to the Houthis.

According to some estimates, the Iranian-backed rebels have captured as much as 130km (81 miles) of the country's strategically important coastline.

It's the group's most impressive military coup for several years, proving that despite a civil war that has lasted 12 years, devastating Saudi air raids and attacks by American, Israeli and British forces, the Houthis remain a force to be reckoned with.

With their opponents stunned and demoralised, it's unlikely the Houthis will be dislodged any time soon.

"Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."

Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" – Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria.

"So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."

Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.

Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal).

"Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally."

"This is as much leverage as a nuclear bomb," he says.

If the Houthis have also taken control of several key islands in the Red Sea, including Perim - which sits in the middle of the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab - then the group's ability to interfere with international shipping will be greatly enhanced.

As the group's actions in the wake of Israel's war on Gaza proved, shipping in the Red Sea is highly vulnerable to Houthi missiles, drones and small attack boats.

"They were able to control what was going in and out of the Bab al-Mandab and up towards Suez without having these territorial gains," Yemen expert Iona Craig told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"But of course now they're controlling the area immediately overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, and this gives them far more leverage."

Shipping companies are likely to be sceptical about the sincerity of a statement released on Friday afternoon, in which the Houthi military said that maritime navigation was "safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels, which have already been subject to a blockade".

In their earlier attacks, the Houthis said they were only targeting vessels linked to Israel, but in fact hit ships with no such connection, including a Norwegian-flagged tanker.

Craig said the Houthis may nevertheless refrain from indiscriminate attacks, fearing a repeat of Operation Rough Rider - six weeks of major US air and naval strikes in the spring of 2025.

"They've already felt the wrath of the US," she said.

But would the US want to get involved anyway?

President Donald Trump's war with Iran is already unpopular. With oil prices creeping back up, it's doubtful that a new front would do much to enhance his approval ratings or his Republican party's chances in November's midterm US elections.

According to the Axios website, appeals for US intervention from the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have so far gone unanswered.

Axios writes that the US "is increasingly concerned about the escalating conflict in Yemen and is working to intensify its support for the kingdom while simultaneously seeking to avoid direct military involvement".

But it's not just the potential threat to the Bab al-Mandab that's causing fear in Saudi Arabia.

Satellite images of an apparent Houthi missile-and-drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline – a vital alternative route for oil exports following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year – point to an effort by Iran's Yemeni allies to add to the economic pressures generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Even if Iran did not directly order the attack, it clearly stands to benefit.

Baraa Shaiban, a researcher and analyst at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, says the origins of the latest upsurge in fighting – the worst since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 - can be traced back to July, when a Houthi delegation returned from the state funeral of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

"Immediately after, the escalation started," he says, "and it looked very clearly that [Iran was] determined to now have a bigger foothold on the Red Sea".

With Yemen teetering on the edge of a return to all-out war, Saudi Arabia anxious about preserving its economic lifeline to the Red Sea and Donald Trump apparently reluctant to get involved, America's conflict with Iran just took on a new and potentially dangerous dimension.

For the people of Yemen, displaced, bombed, starved and impoverished by a dozen years of civil war, recent developments can only make their lives worse.

Breaking.title: 70 Up: Curtain falls on documentary that has captivated Brits for six decades
Breaking.text:
Six decades have passed since Jackie Bassett first appeared on TV aged seven, skipping down the road with her little sister.

It was 1964 and she had been selected by teachers at her east London primary school to appear in a documentary called 7 Up.

The show interviewed 14 seven-year-olds from vastly different socioeconomic backgrounds. Inspired by the Jesuit saying: "Give me the child until he is seven and I will show you the man", it was intended as a one-off - a snapshot of Britain's class system and how it shapes us from a young age.

"They only picked me because I never stopped talking," Jackie told the BBC, with an infectious giggle that hasn't changed since childhood.

Little did she know then, but Jackie was being filmed for a show that would go on to be the longest-running documentary series ever made. In 2024, it was voted the most influential TV show of the past 50 years.

Now the curtain is falling, with the final instalment - 70 Up - airing on ITV this Tuesday.

"We didn't really know what we were doing, we had no idea what was happening," Jackie said of the day the Granada TV crew turned up at her school.

In the first episode, Jackie appeared alongside her friends, Lynn and Sue, as they were asked questions about boys at school and their hopes for the future. Jackie said she would like to marry a boy "that's not got a lot of money, but has got some money".

The nation was also introduced to the likes of wide-eyed Neil, who explained his plans to become either an astronaut or a coach driver; anxious Paul, who ruminated on the idea of one day marrying a woman who made him eat his greens; and pensive Bruce, who said his "heart's desire is to see my daddy who is 6,000 miles away" in Rhodesia.

The first episode was directed by Canadian Paul Almond, with the help of a young researcher named Michael Apted, who was involved in selecting the children.

Apted then decided to follow up on the children seven years later.

"The material was dreadful – as teenagers, they wouldn't say anything," he later said of the second episode, 7 Plus Seven.

"Yet we started to realise the power of the idea; despite the film not being very good, everyone was interested in it."

Apted went on to become a big name in Hollywood, directing blockbusters including James Bond's The World Is Not Enough, but he always returned to the show and said it was his most significant achievement.

Every seven years, millions would tune in for updates on the cast's lives. Neil's dreamy outlook on the world as a child descended into battles with depression, isolation and homelessness, only to turn up as a Liberal Democrat councillor at 42 and then a lay preacher seven years later.

Jackie initially said she did not want children, but by 42 Up was an adoring mother to three boys.

As the series grew in popularity, Apted started receiving push-back from some of the participants, who felt they had been typecast based on their backgrounds.

At 21, Apted asked Jackie - who had recently got married - whether she had met "enough men" before she decided to marry. For the rest of the interview, she mostly looked to the floor while Sue and Lynn answered questions.

It took her 18 years to fully confront Apted over his questioning.

In 49 Up, she told him: "I was really angry… you wouldn't have asked some of the other people in this programme that question. You will edit this programme as you see fit, I've got no control over that."

Recalling the tense exchange, Jackie said she felt Apted could be out of touch, particularly over the changing roles of women in society.

"I think he still thought we were all in the kitchen, as I mentioned to him at 21. I just thought, 'No, come on, it's about time one of us called you out on it, because he never never asked us questions about politics. It was nearly always domestic," she said.

Jackie was not the only cast member to clash with Apted.

John Brisby, who became a leading barrister, declared in 35 Up that the show felt like a "little pill of poison" injected into his veins every seven years and he wished his headmaster had never put him up for the show. He appeared in later series but refused to be interviewed by Apted.

And Charles Furneaux, who later worked at the BBC before becoming commissioning editor at Channel 4, refused to appear after 21 Up following an off-camera argument in which Apted later admitted he went "berserk".

Apted acknowledged flaws with the show, saying it was a "horrible error" to have only four women in a cast of 14 when making the original selection.

Five years ago, Apted passed away, aged 79.

The effect he had on the cast is clear in the final episode.

Despite their differences, Jackie maintains deep affection and respect for the man she said "opened up a world to me that I would never have known".

"I've always said it's a bit like having an uncle in the family. Sometimes you love him and cuddle him to death, and other times you think: I wish he'd just go away.

"He would always, always help anybody and anything."

Nick Hitchon died from cancer in 2023, becoming the second member of the cast to pass away after Lynn Johnson 10 years earlier.

Nick, who was born on a farm in the Yorkshire Dales and famously said he wanted to "find out about the moon and all that" in 7 Up, went on to become a scientist and professor at the University of Wisconsin.

In his obituary, his brother Andrew wrote Nick "was an expert in nuclear fusion who eventually accepted that he would always be best known for appearing in a ground-breaking TV documentary rather than as a scientist".

And does this episode really mark the end?

"I'm not sure any of us will have the energy for it, to be honest," Jackie said. "I think this is the right time to stop, I really do.

"Seventy has got a symmetry to it," she said. "We started at seven, we finished at 70 - and that's it."

Despite all the plaudits, Jackie has always been slightly perplexed as to why the show has made such an impact, but understands how watching their journeys has helped some people make sense of their own.

The series started out being about class but "then they suddenly thought, hang on a minute, this is about life", she said.

"There's somebody on that programme that just about everybody can associate with. And I think that is something that will outlast all of us."

Breaking.title: Anti-migrant activists like Danny Tommo are changing tactics
Breaking.text:
At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham.

The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground.

In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.

In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.

Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.

It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL).

"I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.

The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."

The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".

On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth.

His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normandy in France.

On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings.

"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

Some of Patriot Platform's disruptive, eye-catching tactics seem to have been borrowed from environmental groups like Just Stop Oil. But its leaders are also getting ideas and funding from the growing "Christian nationalism" seen in the United States.

Its organisers say they are building a working-class "voting bloc" to persuade political parties on the right to adopt their agenda.

What sets Patriot Platform apart is the scale and co-ordination of their action, says William Allchorn of Anglia Ruskin University, an expert on far-right movements.

"There hasn't [previously] been co-ordinated mass activism with hundreds of people descending and trying to take matters, as it were, into their own hands," he says.

Thomas spent the summer posting further videos about the group and staging meetings in the North West, Essex, Leicester and Kent. He said he was trying to organise a "mass resistance" movement.

What happened in Dover demonstrated some of his new ways of working. The protesters were almost exclusively male. They arrived in well-organised waves in the backs of lorries. They did not engage with the media, and said little to members of the public whose journeys and weekends they were disrupting.

Then, after a few hours, before the police could get organised, the men all marched off to Dover Priory Station and left. Estimates vary as to how many were there but it looks like between 200 and 500.

The anti-racism group Hope Not Hate said Patriot Platform should be seen "for what it is: a far-right network of men happy to intimidate and inconvenience an entire town for what was effectively a publicity stunt".

Nick Lowles, the group's CEO, said Thomas had "been upfront about his intention to create a 'patriotic army that is able to take control of the United Kingdom'".

At a protest outside the Daily Mail offices in London on Wednesday, Thomas could be seen giving clear instructions to his supporters about his preferred tactics.

"Don't intimidate anyone," he ordered. "No one talk. Keep a distance. Five metres away from police".

Patriot Platform is coming into a crowded space of activists campaigning against immigration. Robinson's is the most high-profile brand. A former close associate of Danny Thomas, Robinson (whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon) has given Patriot Platform public support since Saturday.

But there is also Paul Golding's Britain First, Turning Point UK and the neo-Nazi Patriotic Alternative.

Thomas was once close to Ryan Bridge, the founder of a group called Raise the Colours, who have put up flags in towns across England over the last year.

But the pair have since publicly fallen out, with Thomas telling Bridge in an online rant: "Do I need to stab you in the eye?"

Thomas was jailed for two years in 2016 after he and two others tried to kidnap a man at knifepoint in Portsmouth in a dispute over money linked to drugs.

What seems to be different about Patriot Platform's approach now is that Thomas is explicitly talking about creating a "voting bloc" of supporters to back a yet-to-be decided party, which offers policies closest to what he wants, at the next general election.

"I do not support any political party at this moment in time," he said, adding that once the bloc was established, it would be made "extremely clear" which way the group's vote would go.

It's not clear whether Reform UK would get his backing. In a public confrontation with Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf in Portsmouth on Monday, Thomas complained that Nigel Farage had branded his Dover protest "disgusting".

"The working class do not vote," Thomas said. "We are going to make it a fashionable thing to take all your family members to the voting booth.

"But if your leader keeps slandering people, it's going to push them to other parties."

Waiting in the wings is the new party Restore Britain, launched by Rupert Lowe after he was suspended from Reform UK. On X, the party said it "stands with the patriots peacefully protesting against the invasion".

It is not clear how much support Thomas has. Parties like Reform and Restore will be very aware of the potential power that activists like Thomas and Robinson can now wield with their large social media followings. On X, Robinson has two million followers to Farage's 2.3 million, while Thomas has almost 163,000.

Thomas is trying to raise money for Patriot Platform through a popular American Christian crowdfunding platform. Just below the "Give" and "Share" buttons, there is a "Pray" button.

On the page, Thomas says he is trying to raise £5,000 a month to pay for the likes of transport, boats and a studio. This month alone he has raised around £9,000.

This attempt to build Christianity into the brand is potentially also a way of painting the UK as a Christian country, and Muslim immigrants as outsiders.

As for what comes next for the Patriot Platform after its initial surge in supporters, far-right expert Allchorn thinks it's an unclear picture.

"A lot of these groups don't really have an end goal in mind," he says. "This often comes kind of later on when they are kind of forced to to come up with more concrete proposals and goals."

Breaking.title: The mission to recover Nims Purja's body from Broad Peak
Breaking.text:
As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.

Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.

But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.

The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.

And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him.

"I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"

Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.

Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."

Mingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter.

Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.

The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.

Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers.

Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following.

In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after.

Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant."

But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met".

Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest".

This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart.

Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened.

"That was the last thing he told me. I still regret it."

On 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says.

By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak.

At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains.

The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow.

The group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak".

"We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope.

The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed.

The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall.

By the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life.

But something was bothering him.

One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him.

Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night.

But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak.

Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers.

He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m.

It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong".

Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors.

"I was totally blank," Mingma G recalls in a low voice.

He wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once.

"Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind."

Later that day, Mingma G called off his K2 expedition.

Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back.

They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks.

But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home.

When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'".

Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated.

The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home.

Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says.

The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days.

There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot.

On 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby.

With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down.

The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says.

The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away.

The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four.

Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope.

The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him.

Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall.

"They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived."

The team brought the bodies back down the mountain. They were flown by helicopter to the nearby city of Skardu, then on to the capital Islamabad and finally, home to their families.

Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi's body was found a few days later, as was the body of American climber Mallory Geis. The body of Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa remains on the mountain.

Nims's family say they are deeply grateful to the "extraordinary team led by our brother, Mingma G, who worked in incredibly challenging conditions to bring Nimsdai home".

This recovery operation has stayed with Mingma G. It doesn't compare to any other mission he has done.

As he looks back with deep sorrow, he feels the end of his career could be coming.

Memories of Kilu and Nims - the three of them singing together as they marched up to the summit of a freezing but sunny K2 a few years ago - will always be with him.

But, he says, "I'm not sure if it helps, if the memory helps me to keep climbing or it makes me stop."

Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Breaking.title: I couldn't experience my baby scan but blind parents like me can now feel them
Breaking.text:
When I attended pregnancy scans a decade ago, the best the sonographer could do to involve this blind expectant mum was to turn up the volume on the heartbeat.

But now, parents like me can receive tactile 3D models created from their scans, allowing them to have a special moment with their unborn baby.

Reece Finnegan-Knight, who has been blind since his teens, is one of the first people to experience a 3D-printed model of his baby's scan with his wife, Sophy, as part of a new pilot scheme.

At their routine 12-week scan, Sophy had attempted to describe what she was seeing for Reece, but he struggled to feel involved in the moment.

Afterwards, when the couple showed the sonogram to their loved ones, Reece said it felt like "friends and family knew more about my baby than I did".

But he said the 20-week scan was more positive.

"The sonographer described everything to me, and explained why what she was seeing meant that everything looked good," he says.

They also now have the model of their 20-week scan picture, through the scheme by the charity Guide Dogs.

"I can't stop feeling it to be honest," Reece says.

"It's so nice to be able to fully access something without the need for other people's descriptions or interpretations. It has enough detail that I know what things are and it just makes everything feel more real."

It's an innovation which has made me reflect on my own experiences of pregnancy and parenting.

Before my partially sighted husband and I started trying for kids, I researched absolutely everything it would entail, from how to use specialist apps to read pregnancy test results, to the bells and squeaky shoes I could use to keep tabs on a fast-moving toddler.

I immediately discovered a community of people in my position ready to share their wisdom, and a host of tried and tested workarounds for almost every scenario.

But a decade on, there are even more advances, and I've spoken to other blind parents to find out the best ways they tackle the challenges they face.

For Kim and Sean Randall, who have a teenager and an 11-month-old, the progress of technology is one of the biggest changes they have noticed in the 15 years between the births of their children.

For their youngest child, maternity notes came in an app which could be accessed with a screen reader on their phone, rather than being handwritten in the traditional NHS blue book.

Kim says it put her on more of an equal footing with other expectant parents, and helped her feel more in control.

"I could check the notes, and any test results, when I wanted rather than waiting to have them read to me," she says.

For the 20-week scan, she says Sean had researched the meaning of the different numbers on an ultrasound - like the baby's thigh length or head circumference - and used a specialist AI screen-reading app to have the text read out and the images described.

Some parents say they prefer this method to a 3D model, because they can get more detail from audio description of the image than from physical touch.

But it's not just scans where visually impaired parents can struggle.

Reece, like many blind parents, says he wants to be extra prepared for when the baby comes, "so I don't get in the way or feel like a liability".

"We've been labelling clothes, putting Braille in baby books and organising the baby bag so that I know where everything is," he says.

Kim, meanwhile, runs Facebook and WhatsApp groups for blind mums. Together, we have collated a host of tips and tricks from blind parents over the years for what to do when the baby arrives.

They include things like:

Carry your own folding mat for nappy changes and always have everything you need close at hand

When changing a nappy, if you think you can stop, "keep wiping" - and use barrier cream, because the start of a nappy rash can be hard to feel

Score a raised mark on any syringes or scoops you might use for making up feeds so you know where to fill them to

Use a baby carrier or pram which can be pulled as well as pushed, in case you walk with a guide dog or cane in front of you to get around

Once they start toddling, bells clipped to clothing are a handy way of knowing where they are at home

When weaning, use a wipeable high chair with a waterproof mat underneath, to keep mess contained and know what they've eaten and what's gone on the floor

The Royal National Institute of Blind People , external(RNIB) has also produced guides for expectant parents and those with young children.

They suggest ideas like using baby gates to block off the kitchen when you are removing something from the oven, or the hall when you are answering the door.

For parents who have some but not total visual impairment, Kim says children can be dressed in brightly coloured clothing while out and about so they are easier to spot.

"I put them in feelable clothes so I don't grab the wrong child," says Kim, who has no vision.

"One of my favourites is a shirt with a castle on it. You open the door and there's a dragon inside."

When her eldest started walking, she says "we always held hands, but had a wrist strap connecting us in case she tried to run off".

For me, clothes pegs were always useful for keeping outfits together wherever possible.

Also consider buying socks the same style and colour - matching those is still a nightmare for me a decade later. If two items feel the same but are different colours, cut the label on one of them.

Parents Reece and Sophy are just at the start of their journey, but are making sure they are fully prepared for what lies ahead.

As the due date rapidly approaches, they were given a hospital tour as an accessibility requirement.

For Reece, knowing his way around the maternity ward beforehand means he can be "more independent and able to support Sophy as her birthing partner".

My own children are older now, and I look back at those early years with gratitude for the blind parents before me who figured out the workarounds and gave reassurance when others' attitudes or new challenges caused me to lose confidence.

I now pay that forward whenever possible. For blind parents, that community exists and is ready to be a source of support.

And remember, when you think you can stop, always keep wiping.

Breaking.title: French officials investigate if malicious act caused train derailment
Breaking.text:
Officials in northern France are investigating whether the derailment of a passenger train on Friday evening was the result of a malicious act.

"At this stage, the leading theory is that a piece of rail was present on one of the tracks, potentially causing the derailment. The reason for its presence is unknown," prosecutor Sébastien Gallois said on Saturday.

Local media say 186 passengers were on board the train that was operating between Rouen and Caen in Normandy.

Forty-four people were treated for injuries, including an 18-year-old woman who was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition.

"The train's 'black box' has been seized. Several interviews are scheduled, and a court-appointed expert has been called in," prosecutor Gallois said in a press release.

"The main victim is still in hospital but her life is no longer in danger. The other victims have received care and treatment; they have either been discharged or are about to be."

The Rouen prosecutor's office earlier said the train driver had tested negative for drugs and alcohol.

The train derailed near Cléon, just south of Rouen, shortly before 20:00 (18:00 GMT), and some 140 firefighters and other emergency teams were immediately deployed to the crash scene.

"Suddenly there were a few jolts, and then after about three seconds it got stronger and stronger," Louis, a passenger on the train, told ICI Normandie radio.

"I couldn't stay in my seat anymore. The windows partially shattered, the stones from the track came into the carriage. It was really shocking. I'm still shaking," he added.

Breaking.title: Ukraine faces 'toughest winter' since Russia's full-scale invasion, UN warns
Breaking.text:
Ukraine is facing its "toughest winter" since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, a top United Nations official told the BBC.

Alexander De Croo, head of the UN development agency, said there was a risk of "humanitarian catastrophe" if Russian attacks cut off access to power and water.

Speaking in Ukraine, De Croo – the UN's third most senior official – accused Russia of systematically targeting the country's energy infrastructure. He said there was now a "race against the clock" to repair the power network before winter sets in and temperatures plummet.

Russia and Ukraine have been intensifying aerial attacks in recent months, and both deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure.

Russia has started to use faster, jet-powered drones that are harder to intercept in recent around-the-clock attacks on Ukraine - and in particular Kyiv. Many of the strikes have targeted Ukraine's infrastructure, including businesses, warehouses, factories, petrol stations, as well as energy infrastructure.

Ukraine continues to launch drone strikes deep into Russian territory, largely against gas, oil and business distribution facilities. Both countries deny targeting civilians.

Deadly attacks have resumed after US President Donald Trump sent envoys for talks in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin and in Kyiv with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend.

Five people were killed and 67 others were wounded in a daytime Russian drone strike on a shopping mall in Pavlohrad, a city in Dnipropetrovsk region, on Thursday, Ukrainian officials say. Earlier in the week two other shopping malls were targeted by Russian air strikes, killing two people and injuring 28 people in the attacks on the cities of Zaporizhzhia and Sumy.

Russia reported a Ukrainian seaborne drone attack on the resort city of Sochi overnight on Wednesday, in which 28 people were wounded, as well as three more deaths blamed on Ukrainian attacks.

Two people were also killed earlier this week when Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, which has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict.

A full-scale war has been raging between Russia and Ukraine since Putin launched an invasion more than four and a half years ago.

De Croo, a former prime minister of Belgium, told the BBC: "This winter is going to be the toughest one since the war".

He said Ukraine started "from a very weak base going into this winter". He added the UN were "very, very worried... about what this winter could become."

The concerns are driven by what De Croo said was Russia's "very systematic" targeting of civilian and energy infrastructure.

"This is petrol stations, it's shopping malls, it's business centres, but it's especially energy infrastructure, energy transmission lines, and so on. There is absolutely no justification for that," he said.

This could lead a "worst-case scenario" where people struggled to access energy to run heating, and water and sewage systems stopped working.

"With the temperatures that you would get here that would lead to circumstances which would be really close to humanitarian catastrophe," De Croo said.

Winter temperatures in Ukraine can drop to -20C.

If power supplies and critical infrastructure were severely damaged it could lead to "quite some human suffering", De Croo said.

Under efforts to prepare Ukraine for winter the UN Development Programme is helping to rebuild parts of its energy system that were damaged last winter. It is also establishing more sustainable and decentralised energy plants, which are less vulnerable to attack.

De Croo said completing the difficult and dangerous work was "almost an impossible task".

"They are reconstructing these sites under constant, constant air alarms. And they know that they are working at a site which is a target," he said. "So you try to reconstruct, but part of your day you can't work because it's just too dangerous."

Breaking.title: Kenyan crackdown on foreign traders prompts fear: 'It's like a dog set loose on us'
Breaking.text:
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.

During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.

"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.

"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."

President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.

During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.

Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.

"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."

Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.

Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.

"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.

"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.

In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.

She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.

"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.

In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.

Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.

Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.

Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.

He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.

The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.

The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.

Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.

Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.

The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.

Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.

Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.

He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.

For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."

The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.

Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.

Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.

Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.

He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.

Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".

The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.

In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.

"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.

"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."

Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.

He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".

"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?

"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."

For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.

"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.

Breaking.title: Death toll from Philippines ferry fire climbs to 35, with dozens still missing
Breaking.text:
The Philippine Coast Guard says it has recovered 30 bodies from the wreckage of a ferry that caught fire this week, bringing the total death toll to 35.

More than 130 people were on board the MV June Aster when the blaze erupted on Wednesday as it neared its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, after departing from Manila.

Forty-three people were rescued, with many receiving treatment in hospital, and searches continue for more than 50 people who remain unaccounted for.

The country's coast guard says more bodies remain on the boat, which they were unable to board until Friday due to toxic fumes and lingering heat.

In a press conference, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said most bodies had been retrieved from the sleeping area of the boat, which had been making a 22-hour journey.

"Agencies are currently undertaking the proper recovery and identification of the remains in accordance with established procedures," Cayabyab said.

"We recognise the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident."

Earlier, the coast guard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that the fire started in the cargo hold. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.

A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat told the BBC he had heard frantic cries onboard when the fire erupted, and was trampled by panicked people as he tried to escape.

The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.

The vessel was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members.

Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry.

"Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.

Breaking.title: France lifts alcohol content limit on champagne after record heatwaves
Breaking.text:
Champagne lovers may find themselves getting tipsy more quickly after French producers have been given the go-ahead to raise the alcohol content in a bottle of bubbly for the first time following this summer's record heatwave.

Winemakers can temporarily produce champagne with an alcohol content of up to 15% - above the 13% cap, industry officials have said.

The extreme heat and drought produced grapes with exceptionally higher sugar levels. Yeast converts sugar into alcohol during fermentation.

France's Champagne region also saw its earliest-ever harvest due to the weather, something that could become the norm "in 10 to 15 years" because of climate change, according to the Comite Champagne industry association.

The temporary increase in champagne's alcohol content is only expected to affect a small number of wines, a spokeswoman for the Comite Champagne told the BBC.

During the second fermentation process, which gives champagne its bubbles, "a very small number of wines from this harvest could have slightly exceeded the regulatory limit of 13%, reaching around 13.1% or 13.2%".

"Therefore a decision was made to exceptionally and temporarily increase the regulatory limit to 15% - only for this year," she said.

The first grapes were cut in early August and the harvest expanded by the middle of the month, "the earliest ever recorded in Champagne", the association said.

"The 2026 growing season will be remembered as one of the most unusual in Champagne's history, marked by severe spring frosts of historic intensity, an exceptionally early flowering period and five heatwaves throughout the summer." it added.

Speaking in the Times newspaper, Stéphane Vignon, a producer in Verzenay said: "The Mediterranean climate is moving north. This is year one of a new cycle. It's unlikely to be every year, but it will happen again".

Higher-strength champagne is unlikely to be an obvious selling point, warned Jane Anson, a wine columnist and author based in Bordeaux.

She told the Times: "Today people increasingly prefer lower-alcohol

"The battle between what consumers want and what nature provides must be very stressful for producers."

The 2026 vintage is unlikely to hit shelves until 2028 as champagne must age for at least 15 months.

Business.title: Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record
Business.text:
Reform UK has received a second £36m donation in as many days, as cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne says he has matched a record-breaking donation announced late on Friday.

Harborne wrote in the Telegraph, external that his "competitive spirit" had inspired him to equal Ben Delo's donation - the largest ever given to a UK political party.

The Thailand-based entrepreneur said he expected "nothing personally" in return aside from "a party that is ready for government".

Reform said the £72m would be used to hire "the brightest and best minds to work on policy and the most comprehensive plan for government ever".

The £72m from these two donations is more than the total received by all UK political parties last year, which stood at just over £69m.

Reform leader Nigel Farage said Harborne and Delo's "generosity" meant the party would "now be able to fight and win the next general election on a level playing field".

A Reform UK spokesman added: "We will now also be able to hire up to 400 campaign managers in every target constituency. We are now on election footing."

Harborne has already donated millions to Reform and Farage, who is currently under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a £5m cash gift from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.

Farage has argued that he was under no obligation to register the "purely private" gift, as it was unrelated to his parliamentary or political activities.

The party is also facing scrutiny over its finances after a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week showed two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations.

The Metropolitan Police has said it is investigating, while the party denies any wrongdoing.

The force is also looking into donations given to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell, as well as a company controlled by its deputy leader Richard Tice.

Harborne wrote on Saturday that he had "already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life", while Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage".

"A start-up party needs more money than can be provided by membership fees alone, to build and sustain itself and be ready for government," he said.

Harborne and Delo's donations mark the largest sums received by a UK political party since they had to begin declaring them in 2001.

Delo, who also announced his donation in a Telegraph op-ed, said he was giving the money away because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field".

Addressing the recent scrutiny of Reform's finances, he said: "My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."

Last year, he was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMEX, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

However, the Labour government has introduced a £100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, and plans to introduce a similar one for those who have recently returned to the UK.

There were nine donations of £1m or more to political parties in 2025. The largest was £9m given to Reform UK by Harborne.

Labour had five donations of £1m or more - totalling nearly £10m - and the Conservatives had three of £1m each.

Labour said Reform and Farage still had "serious questions" to answer about their finances.

Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said Reform were "drowning" in "sleaze and scandal",.

She added: "It's time Farage and Reform came clean with the public, fully co-operated with the ongoing police investigations and prove they're not just in it for themselves."

Rachel Millward, deputy leader of the Green Party, told BBC News it wanted a cap on donations from individuals of £500,000.

She said the donations to Reform were "absolutely staggering amounts", adding: "What I am very frustrated about is the influence of extreme wealth and the super rich. What I want to see is people in politics representing the needs of their communities and ordinary people."

After news of Delo donation emerged, Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said Farage wanted to "bring Trump's America to our shores by buying his way into power".

She said: "Andy Burnham needs to introduce a cap on political donations. Our democracy depends on it."

Business.title: Ryanair boss O'Leary defends 'high-fare rapists' airlines remarks
Business.text:
Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists".

Speaking to journalists, O'Leary said some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe".

O'Leary doubled-down on his choice of words when asked about them at the time, and later refused to apologise when the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for apology, in a letter seen by the BBC.

Ireland's deputy premier Simon Harris said it was "clearly an inappropriate use of language" and that O'Leary "should have moved to rectify it".

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander told UK radio outlet LBC that victims of rape are "not going to be rushing to book tickets with him, let's be honest".

O'Leary made the comments on Thursday while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders.

Asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate, he said: "Absolutely."

"British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he added.

Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime".

Following O'Leary's comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh wrote to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments.

She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said".

She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise.

"I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote.

In response, O'Leary said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape."

He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training".

It is not the first time O'Leary has offended people while talking about his business.

In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists", external in a row over airport charges.

He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories".

Business.title: US prices remain high as fuel costs squeeze household budgets
Business.text:
Prices in the US rose by 3.4% in the year to August, with the cost of living pushed up by higher gasoline prices, official figures show.

The overall inflation rate was unchanged from July, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

It comes ahead of the Federal Reserve making its latest interest rate decision next week, with growing expectations they will be increased in a bid to slow the rate at which prices are rising.

US household budgets have come under mounting pressure, especially at the fuel pumps, with a gallon of diesel hitting a new all-time high of more than $6 on average on Friday.

The spike in fuel prices has been driven by higher global oil prices, caused by supply disruptions as a result of the US-Iran war. The price of benchmark Brent crude oil is hovering above $100 a barrel following recent escalations in the conflict.

As well as directly driving up costs at the pumps, higher oil prices can also make transporting goods more expensive. Such costs can be passed down to consumers through steeper prices for food and other staples, pushing up the overall cost of living.

The BLS said gasoline prices rose 3.9% last month alone, accounting for more than a third of inflation overall. Wages are also failing to keep up with the rising cost of living, with separate figures showing real average hourly earnings fell by 0.3% over the past year.

There are increasing expectations that interest rates will be hiked given the current inflation picture, strong jobs market and President Donald Trump saying he does not think oil prices will come down until the war with Iran ends, which he expects to happen after November's elections.

Fed chair Kevin Warsh has been tight-lipped on any future decisions, but his comments that the central bank's focus should be on slowing price rises has further fuelled expectations of a rise.

According to data from CME Group, 85% of traders are now betting on rates being raised by a quarter percentage point next week.
