articles.title: US Open final 2026: Why Aryna Sabalenka has extra motivation to beat Elena Rybakina in New York
articles.text:
Aryna Sabalenka was fully aware she would have to win the US Open to stand any chance of stopping Elena Rybakina overtaking her as world number one.

Even that would not necessarily be enough. And as the pair prepare to meet in Saturday's final, Sabalenka knows her 99-week stay at the top of the world rankings is at an end.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina is assured of replacing Sabalenka at the top of the rankings, guaranteeing that by reaching the semi-finals.

Having also beaten the Belarusian to win this year's Australian Open title, Rybakina now has the opportunity to inflict further damage.

But that provides extra motivation for Sabalenka before their fourth meeting of the year.

"It is going to be red rag to a bull for her - she is not going to be happy," said former British number one Annabel Croft on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Now she has the opportunity to end this year on a high."

Sabalenka, who has beaten Rybakina in Indian Wells and Miami since the Melbourne final, still has history in her sights as she bids to become only the third woman in the Open era to win the New York singles title three years in a row.

The four-time Grand Slam champion's victory over American third seed Jessica Pegula in the semi-finals was her finest display in months, playing with a fire and freedom that had been missing previously.

Afterwards, Sabalenka played down the significance of losing her ranking, joking she did not care about it.

But she clearly does. Sabalenka's coach Anton Dubrov said as much when he spoke about how the issue has been hanging over her.

"I actually like this [losing the ranking] happened. It's ended and it's extra fuel," Dubrov said.

"There is no more extra draining [of mental energy] or thinking about it.

"There's a next chapter right now. You have to chase again. It's extra motivation for you. Just go and get it."

Sabalenka might have arrived in New York as the two-time defending champion, but there were concerns about her game and mindset.

Over the past five months, the 28-year-old had lost a series of matches from strong positions against opponents she was expected to beat.

The most notable was in the French Open quarter-finals. Sabalenka held a commanding set and a double break lead against 25th seed Diana Shnaider before capitulating to a 3-6 7-5 6-0 defeat.

Earlier in the clay-court season, Sabalenka blew six match points against Hailey Baptiste in Madrid and let slip a first-set lead over Sorana Cirstea in Rome, demonstrating a lack of mental focus that she had not shown on the WTA Tour for a long time.

A chink of vulnerability was still apparent during this North American hard-court swing, when she held clear advantages against 20-year-old Czech opponent Sara Bejlek at the Cincinnati Open before losing in straight sets.

But there was no panic for Sabalenka or her team, says her high performance coach Jason Stacy.

"We all understand that this is just part of the thing," Stacy said.

"We just give her space to be herself, help her figure out what might work for her right now.

"Giving her that freedom, but also knowing that she has the guidance of all of us, I think that just gives her a power that few are lucky enough to have."

articles.title: England vs Pakistan player ratings: Has Jordan Cox given selectors food for thought?
articles.text:
Emilio Gay - 6 - A gritty Test-best of 60 in tricky batting conditions in the first innings looked to have gone some way towards securing his place on the plane for a winter tour of South Africa, only for a duck next time round to bring back some uncertainty. (Series - 6)

Ben Duckett - 2 - A miserable end to the summer for the opener who will now come under some scrutiny. Made 11 and zero in this match and finishes this three-Test series well down the averages with a disappointing 44 runs at 8.8. (Series - 2)

Jordan Cox - 7 - A cheap dismissal in the first innings but made a nerveless unbeaten 59 to take the sting out of Pakistan after a wobble in the chase. A particularly impressive effort with the gloves - taking five dismissals - after being called upon to keep following Jamie Smith's injury may have given the selectors food for thought in the role. (Series - 7)

Joe Root - 7 - Question marks over his captaincy during Pakistan's second innings, but got England over the line with 62 not out. A 10th lbw in 14 innings suggests a technical issue which still needs to be ironed out by England's all-time leading run-scorer. (Series - 7)

Harry Brook - 7 - Batted with real discipline and focus at a time when Pakistan had a foothold in the game on day one. His most mature Test knock this year. Ran himself out on 75 when a century beckoned but forgivable given the application he showed earlier. Finishes as leading run-scorer in the series with 215 runs at 53.75. (Series - 8)

Dan Lawrence - 7 - Having been shunted around the order the Surrey all-rounder batted with the kind of confidence to suggest he might deserve a sustained run in the middle during a measured 65. Bowling underused but a not-too-shabby batting average of 46.75 will help his winter touring prospects. (Series - 7)

Jamie Smith - 6 - Not quite back to his fluent best but will be satisfied to notch up useful half-centuries in consecutive Tests. Kept reasonably well in Pakistan's first innings before a finger injury kept him off the field in the second. (Series - 6)

Gus Atkinson - 6 - Wicketless in the first innings and it initially looked like it was going to be another hard-luck tale. However, he shook off the weariness and a change to the City End allowed him to pocket three wickets to lighten his mood. (Series - 5)

Jofra Archer - 7 - Took a bit of tap in the second innings but bowled with plenty of zip and aggression throughout. A brutal ball to dismiss Saud Shakeel was a reminder of his menace. England will be desperate to keep him fit and firing during a pivotal 12 months. (Series - 8)

Ollie Robinson - 8 - Is there anyone better with a Dukes ball in English conditions? Another masterclass in control. England's tone-setter finishes the series with 21 wickets at a miserly 8.76. A breezy half-century on day two also entertained the crowd. (Series - 9)

Josh Tongue - 7 - Mopped up the tourists' lower order in the first innings with 4-42. Healthy returns in all three Tests - 19 wickets in all - and continues to look a vital cog in the machine. (Series - 8)

Azan Awais - 7 - Still finding his feet at Test level. Made a battling 59 off 84 balls in the second innings, after Pakistan were reduced to 0-2, and looks a player worth persisting with.

Saim Ayub - 1 - Called up for this Test after wholesale changes to the Pakistan side and looked drastically undercooked having not played a first-class fixture since October last year. Almost inevitably he bagged a pair. Scrapes a point for leaving the CPL at the drop of a hat to turn up.

Abdullah Shafique - 1 - Two half-centuries in the series but under leaden skies he was easy meat for Robinson and snared by the Sussex slayer for three and nought.

Shan Masood - 8 - A tame dismissal in the first innings but rolled up his sleeves second time around as he manufactured a composed and defiant 95 to top score for the tourists.

Babar Azam - 6 - Provided a reminder that with bat in hand, on his day, he is up there with the best players in the world to watch. A classy 76 was too little, too late, and as a polarising figure in Pakistan cricket might feel the heat in his role as captain.

Saud Shakeel - 6 - Rode his luck on occasions as he top-scored in the first innings with 43 then made 29 before being on the end of rasping bouncer from Archer. Finished Pakistan's leading run-scorer in the series with 204 at 34.00.

Ghazi Ghori - 2 - A largely unremarkable debut with the bat - scores of four and 16 - and struggled keeping wicket when he had to stand up to the stumps for large periods, leaking 18 byes.

Mohammad Imran - 6 - The most economical of Pakistan's bowlers who brought some vital control to curtail England's free scoring.

Razaullah Khan - 9 - A star is born. The 21-year-old brought a bit of bite to the Pakistan attack and was reminiscent of a young Waqar Younis as he took 4-148 in the first innings. Yet it was a mesmerising innings of 81 with the bat, featuring a joint-best nine sixes, which left an indelible impression.

Mohammad Ali - 5 - Hunted for wickets and beat the bat on a number of occasions but lacked the necessary consistency and control. Needs to iron out his no-ball issue which cost him Root's wicket in the second innings.

Muhammad Abbas - 7 - Pakistan's 'Mr Dependable' kept stoically plugging away as he shouldered much of the bowling burden for the tourists at the age of 36. Made useful lower-order runs to help force England to bat again, then got the ball talking on day four to give the hosts a fright.

articles.title: Garcia vs Benn: WBC welterweight title fight predictions from fighters and pundits
articles.text:
Conor Benn returns to welterweight for the first time since April 2022 to challenge WBC champion Ryan Garcia in Las Vegas.

The 29-year-old Briton is bidding for the crowning moment of his 10-year professional career at T-Mobile Arena.

Benn has won 25 of his 26 fights as a professional and would emulate his father, Nigel, by claiming a WBC title with another victory.

Garcia, 28, is making the first defence of his belt after beating Mario Barrios by decision in February.

The American has picked up 25 victories in his 28-fight career, earning 20 of those wins by knockout, while losing two, with one no-contest.

Live text commentary will begin on Sunday, 13 September at 03:00 BST on the BBC Sport website and app.

BBC Sport spoke to figures from the boxing world to get their predictions for the bout.

"This is a really good fight and it's not as one-sided as everyone thinks. I believe Conor Benn's heart is going to come into question and he's going to have to climb off the floor a couple of times.

"If Garcia has taken this lightly in any way he will lose, but he's in great shape and is saying the right things in the build-up. But I'm still going for a Conor Benn knockout inside eight rounds."

"I thought Benn had a fair chance due to his tenacity and Garcia has quit in fights before. But as the fight is getting closer I think Benn is a big underdog and it's Garcia's fight to lose.

"Benn looked terrible in a catchweight - 3lb above the welterweight limit - last time out against an ageing Regis Prograis, who was injured and had only one good leg, and he couldn't put a dent in him.

"He looks like he's struggled with the weight cut and I don't get a good feeling, so I'll go with a comfortable Garcia win."

Prediction - Garcia

"We know Benn can be tenacious and has power but I don't think he'll be the same fighter he was in the two fights against Chris Eubank Jr. Benn didn't look great in his last fight against Regis Prograis, so you have to give favour to Garcia.

"Garcia has speed, power and patience. Benn will force the pace and I think he walks on to a shot. I'll go with Garcia to get the stoppage inside five rounds."

Prediction - Garcia

"I think Ryan Garcia gets it done - and early. Conor Benn will come out like a steam train and that could be a problem.

"Garcia has the hand speed and serious experience around the ring - he's been doing this for longer than Benn - which might be a bit too much.

"Garcia to win between rounds four and seven, but it should be a fun fight for five or six rounds."

Prediction - Garcia

articles.title: Shelton tips Tiafoe at US Open to move one win from ending 23-year drought
articles.text:
For 23 years they have come and gone. Andy Roddick tried again. Andre Agassi made one final run. James Blake, Mardy Fish, Sam Querrey, John Isner, Tommy Paul and Taylor Fritz all carried the hopes of American men’s tennis deep into the second week of major championships, only to thrash against the ceiling of the sport’s European hegemony time and again.

Now Ben Shelton gets his chance. The fearless 23-year-old from Atlanta surged into his first career grand slam final on a feverish Friday night at the US Open, completing a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 fightback over Frances Tiafoe in a pulsating all-American semi-final beneath the lights of Arthur Ashe Stadium. The result leaves him one victory from becoming the first man from the United States to win one of the sport’s four bedrock tournaments since Roddick triumphed here in 2003.

Shelton, the No 8 seed, will face top-seeded Alexander Zverev of Germany in Sunday’s final after turning back a fast start from the 11th-seeded Tiafoe with his devastating serve, landing 75% of his first deliveries and pounding 20 aces before breaking at the last possible moment to avoid a fourth-set tiebreak.

“It’s amazing to be in this position,” Shelton said. “Obviously we’re not done here. The job is not finished. Super excited to get another opportunity to go out there and show my best on Sunday.”

A full house understood the assignment from the first ball. Gone was the ambient drone of chatter that so often hangs over night sessions inside the world’s biggest tennis stadium. Instead, nearly 24,000 spectators were dialed-in on every point, roaring equally for both players as the momentum ebbed and flowed over more than three absorbing hours.

Tiafoe struck first at the business end of an otherwise straightforward first set. Shelton was serving at four-all, 30-love when he abruptly lost his bearings, dropping four of the next five points and double-faulting on break point. Tiafoe coolly held at love to serve out the opening set after 45 minutes.

Shelton’s response was immediate, breaking at love for 2-0 in the second. Tiafoe broke back straight away, but the younger American increasingly leaned on the howitzer first serve that has powered his rapid ascent into the sport’s elite. Serving at three-all, he uncorked missiles of 125mph, 144mph, 139mph and 140mph in succession, the last two aces. He broke in the next game and served out the set with a first serve topping out at 149mph.

The third shifted into a more attritional affair. Tiafoe survived break points at one-all after a series of extended rallies but could not escape at two-all. Shelton crushed a series of backhand winners to break at love before forcing Tiafoe into the deep waters of an extraordinary 15-minute, 20-point service game at 3-5. Tiafoe saved three set points but blinked on the fourth, dumping a forehand into the net to move within a set of going out.

“His game is starting to get more polished,” Tiafoe said. “Instead of just being a shot maker, he’s actually staying tough in the rallies.”

The 28-year-old’s best opportunity to turn the match came immediately in the fourth. Shelton fell behind 15-40 in the opening game only to erase one break point with a 140mph ace and another with a 144mph serve that Tiafoe couldn’t handle. From there both men traded holds through five-all, seemingly bound for a tiebreak that might have forced a decider.

That’s when Shelton pounced. After holding for 6-5, he won a pair of extended rallies to reach love-30 on Tiafoe’s serve, then took the next point to earn three match points. Tiafoe saved the first, but a double-fault on the second brought the stadium to a hush as the curtain dropped after 3hr 16min.

Shelton said he had been surprised by his composure as the finish line approached. “I was honestly shocked with how calm I was out there today, especially towards the end of the match,” he said. “Calm, confident, focused. I think that that’s what it takes to be in these positions and win at the highest level.”

He becomes the first Black American man to reach the US Open singles final since Arthur Ashe in 1972 and the first Black American man to make the final at any grand slam since MaliVai Washington at Wimbledon 30 years ago. Afterwards he insisted he had managed to keep the enormity of the occasion at arm’s length. “Yes, I can think about how cool this moment is and what I’m playing for,” he said. “At the end of the day, I’m here in New York, I’m hanging out with my team, I’m with my homies playing a little bit of tennis and I’ve been able to downplay the moment pretty well.”

Shelton betrayed no signs of fatigue from the grueling five-set quarter-final win over defending champion Carlos Alcaraz that ended at 3.33am on Wednesday morning. That had marked his first victory over a top-three opponent after 17 defeats and ended Alcaraz’s 18-match winning streak at the majors.

Tiafoe had survived an epic of his own, scratching back from two sets down and two points from elimination to defeat Alex Michelsen in a final-set tiebreaker. But for the third time in five years, his US Open ended in at the semi-final stage. “That’s why I just want to win it, man,” Tiafoe said. “The love is incredible. It’s something that gives me definitely tears in my eyes from a kid starting how I did, and the love I have here is crazy.”

Shelton, who won the NCAA singles title at the University of Florida in 2022, reached the Australian Open quarter-finals only four months after turning pro and the last four at the US Open later that year. But he has spent the intervening years working tirelessly to add dimensions to a game once built almost entirely around his serve, making a quantum leap in 2026 while stacking titles in Dallas, Munich, Stuttgart and Montreal.

He pointed specifically to his return game, baseline stability, concentration and even sleeping habits as evidence of that evolution. “I feel that I’m a different player. I feel like I have so many more tools. I feel like I know my identity, am comfortable in my own skin, and I know what it takes for me to be playing top-level tennis.”

His father and coach, Bryan Shelton, offered a similar assessment. “Ben came on to the tour, everything happened so fast. His game wasn’t completely formed. It still isn’t,” he said. “A lot of these guys are well put together when they show up out here, and Ben wasn’t.”

That development, the elder Shelton said, has accelerated over the past 12 months. “He’s become more mature and more disciplined on the court. He’s willing to suffer a little bit in the rallies and go deeper and really use his athleticism.”

One last hurdle remains. Shelton has never beaten Zverev, who eased past Karen Khachanov in Friday’s first semi-final, coming up short in all five of their previous matches during a 16-month span across 2024 and 2025. Sunday will mark their first meeting at a grand slam. The form sheet didn’t appear to bother him.

“Problem-solving has been the name of the game here,” Shelton said. “I‘m looking forward to the challenge, being able to problem-solve on Sunday. I know what I’m up against, and I’m also the most confident I’ve ever been in my game.”

Manchester United: Manchester United supporters’ group The Red Army has said there will be no flag display ahead of Sunday’s derby against Manchester City as part of a protest which follows the club’s investigation into ticket touting.

On Thursday, United revealed they had banned 685 season tickets following a contentious probe which had been condemned by many fans and supporter groups, with protests already planned for Sunday afternoon.

The Red Army said they will make their own views known by removing their regular flag display in the Stretford End and replacing it with a single banner above the players’ tunnel which will read: “The way you treat us is a disgrace.”

In a statement, the group said: “This isn’t a ‘TRA’ message, it’s a message on behalf of every genuine fan group, match-going supporter, supporters’ club and fan representative who has either contacted us directly or been negatively impacted by the recent behaviour of the club.

“It’s an honest, heartfelt cry for recognition from the maligned, vilified, and misrepresented beating heart of our football club – the generational match-going supporters. Neither is this solely a ‘Manchester United’ problem, this is a league-wide crisis that should be addressed at every club, regardless of rivalries and history. Without drastic changes, there will be no rivalries in the future vision for football shared by the decision makers.”

In the statement, the Red Army called for match-going supporters to be prioritised in the club’s fan engagement process. On Thursday, United released an update on their investigation into touting, revealing that 685 accounts have been subject to a ban while 464 supporters received a reduced sanction or final warning.

The club said the investigation had identified 1,617 accounts that required further review due to “unusual activity”. Of those stripped of season tickets, 113 failed to respond to requests for further information, 73 did not appeal and 499 received bans upheld by an independent appeals panel.

A club statement read: “Bans were issued where there was significant misuse of the ticketing system for financial gain. This included the operation of organised ticketing networks, which were controlling, selling and distributing tickets from hundreds of accounts.”

The 1958 supporters’ group responded by calling for fans to “stand united” against the “season ticket ban fiasco” in a protest ahead of the derby, saying a “line has been crossed”.

Fans have been asked to gather outside the Bishop Blaize pub near Old Trafford at 3pm.

articles.title: What can halt Fifa’s authoritarian turn under Infantino? Change from the outside
articles.text:
The 2026 World Cup was a whirling swirl of scintillating soccer that prompted much-needed conversations about the vitality of diaspora, the fortitude of the underdog, the power of sport. In a world fractured along myriad cultural axes floating in an entertainment system dominated by on-demand content, the tournament provided a moment, perhaps unlike any other event, that brought together people from different backgrounds to simultaneously experience something meaningful.

After the tournament concluded, Fifa president Gianni Infantino dropped a political pipebomb into the after-party, proposing to privatize the World Cup by injecting $20bn in private capital, with an assist from JP Morgan and Thrive Capital, the investment vehicle orchestrated by Joshua Kushner, brother to Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

Turns out, Infantino hadn’t just been sucking up to Trump the whole time – from hand-delivering the confected Fifa peace prize to obliging him with the red card reversal heard ’round the world – ostensibly to ensure the World Cup money spigot remained winched wide open. Apparently, Infantino was also studying Trump’s nepotism-flecked smash-and-grab techniques. Not unlike the Trump administration nixing energy-project grants for states “based solely” on whether they supported him in the 2024 presidential election, football associations that backed Infantino’s private-equity scheme would get more money while those that disagreed would receive less. And just as Trump and the rightwing media ecosystem have destabilized the very notion of truth in US political discourse, Fifa subverted the notion of fairness when it nullified the red card for a US player.

But something deeper and even more important is going on. Amid the rising tide of authoritarianism around the world, including in the US under Trump, Fifa under Infantino has itself become increasingly dictatorial. Although Fifa claims it acts “in full respect” of its self-trumpeted “democratic and governance principles”, and that its president’s private-equity fever dream was “about the democratization of football worldwide”, the reality is that Fifa emulates the dictatorships before whom Infantino so readily genuflects. Many within the governing body learned about the privatization gambit through the news rather than proper consultation (just as they had heard of Infantino’s decision to hand Trump the peace prize). Although Fifa statutes limit presidents to “no more than three terms of office”, and Infantino was first elected in 2016 and then re-elected – unopposed by acclamation – in 2019 and 2023, he has declared that he could run again in 2027. Infantino is infamous for besmirching journalists and avoiding press conferences. Tough questions are signs of reporters “spreading hate”. For him, information is meant to flow unidirectionally, cascading from on high.

What can be done? Yes, it’s past time to “give Fifa’s boss the boot”, as a US Soccer vice-president put it. But despite Infantino’s spectacular miscalculations and dictatorial shifts, those who have the power to “boot” him have instead made him the frontrunner in next year’s election. Although soccer’s regional governing bodies in Europe (Uefa), Asia (AFC), as well as North, Central America and the Caribbean (Concacaf) have publicly rebuked Infantino, with Europe even threatening to boycott international competitions, fissures have emerged: Mexico, Qatar and several Asian national associations have broken ranks to signal support for the beleaguered Infantino. The Confederation of African Football (CAF), which represents 54 countries, “unanimously reconfirmed its support” for Infantino, who needs only 106 votes to survive his re-election bid next March. Dislodging Infantino is an uphill fight.

That’s because Fifa’s patronage system is a powerful sedative for dissent: it distributes millions to football associations around the globe under a system of clientelism grounded in fidelity and orchestrated with scant public oversight. This is soccer symbiosis awash in cash and lacking accountability.

Even though Fifa’s proposed privatization could have hurt players, fans and clubs alike, plenty of federations were ready to support it. Sure, private equity has an ignominious record of acquiring holdings with social value, stripping them for parts and leaving a husk of what once was. Exhibit A: sports media. Exhibit B: hospitals. Making football into Exhibit C would not only have risked destroying the world’s most popular sport. It would have been a crime against collective joy. Nevertheless, administrators around the world were happy to back the gambit. This is a testament to the power of that patronage system, built up over decades by successive presidents, from João Havelange to Sepp Blatter to Gianni Infantino.

The top candidates to replace Infantino are freighted with cumbersome baggage. Victor Montagliani rose to become head of Concacaf and a Fifa Council vice-president despite controversial handlings of scandals and partnerships. Another possibility, Fifa Council member Nasser Al-Khelaifi of Qatar, stated that he had “no ambition, no intention and no interest in the Fifa role”. Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, top man at the Asian Football Confederation, already lost to Infantino back in 2016 and has long been dogged by allegations of human-rights violations in Bahrain, which he denies. Lise Klaveness, who heads the Norwegian FA, would bring principle and panache to the presidency – and she has a strong record of standing up to Infantino – but she is essentially unelectable in an organization drenched in sexism.

Let’s be clear: change at Fifa must come from outside the organization. For too long, Fifa has monitored itself. The 2026 World Cup and its aftermath demonstrate unequivocally that Fifa requires independent oversight, toothy regulation carried out by governments and NGOs dedicated to preserving the people’s game as a social good.

Toward that end, FairSquare, the London-based nonprofit human-rights organization on whose advisory board I serve, recently launched a “Reboot Fifa” campaign to declare Infantino ineligible for the March election and to create the biggest-ever class-action complaint against Infantino for openly violating Fifa’s own governing statutes on political neutrality by consistently cozying up to Trump. Donning a red Maga-style cap with “45—47” and “USA” emblazoned on it at a Board of Peace meeting cannot be considered “Fifa remain[ing] neutral in matters of politics”.

Infantino’s clumsy overstepping has galvanized calls for reform and created a chance to reject authoritarianism creep.

articles.title: Solheim Cup golf 2026: Europe take charge against USA after day two foursomes – live
articles.text:
Andrea Lee has joined Yealimi Noh at the party. Her 15 foot birdie at 13 takes the US pair 2UP on Lottie Woad and Charley Hull. It’s only the third counting score made by Lee today and the first that has won a hole.

Maja Stark has drained another sensational shot. “Awesome,” cries team mate Julia Lopez Ramirez as the Swede’s rollercoaster putt at 15 drops. Lauren Coughlin matches her birdie from four feet. The match is hurrying to a conclusion.

2UP Stark/Grant v Khang/Coughlin (15)

Woad/Hull v Noh/An. Lee 1UP (12)

Nadaud/Maguire v Zhang/Kim 3UP (11)

1UP Ciganda/Boutier v Kupcho/Duncan (11)

Linn Grant loves a home Solheim Cup. She went 3-2-0 on debut in Spain, 0-4-0 in Virginia in 2024, and now she’s firing again. 2-0-0 until lunchtime, 2UP in the top match and she’s played a great shot into the par-three 15th. Huge smile on her face and entirely justified in a noisy corner of the course.

Updated at 10.57 EDT

The party feel here in Den Bosch is appropriate. The city has a famous annual carnival which transforms it into a village called Oeteldonk. Yes, for one week it has a completely different name.

The carnival history stretches back to the Middle Ages. The Solheim Cup is a little younger - it was first held in 1990.

Can Lottie Woad add to the vibe? She has a birdie putt at 12 to pull level with Yealimi Noh and Andrea Lee … but it hits the hole and spins out. Carnival cancelled. Only briefly. Celine Boutier chips in for birdie at 10. It’s giddy stuff.

There is a lot of noise on the course currently. And Morgan Pressel notes that the holes are very tight at this point on the back nine. I was out there earlier and it’s true. There are vantage points that allow you to watch two holes at once. The fans are thriving on it.

Rose Zhang slams a 10 foot birdie putt at 11 into the hole. She’s now 3UP with Auston Kim on Europe’s Irish-French combo of Leona Maguire and Nastasia Nadaud.

An eagle-3 for Rose Zhang allows her and Auston Kim to edge 2UP on Leona Maguire and Nastasia Nadaud. Zhang has struggled a little this week, perhaps being a little careful having come into the week with injury concerns.

The other injury concern of the week was Angel Yin who has played just once and is currently on the range trying to find something for the singles.

Maja Stark makes birdie at 13, the third in a row for the Swedes. Big roars. And plenty, too, when the Americans cannot match it. She and Linn Grant now lead 2UP in the top match.

There’s a lovely sense of the Surrey heathland about Bernardus Golf. Nowhere more so than the par-three 11th hole. The trees, the heather, the little ditch, the grass colour. Lottie Woad’s family know it. “It’s like Hankley Common,” they said this morning. But she hasn’t quite clicked on land that ought to make her feel right at home.

On the green, Woad and Charley Hull miss birdie putts. So does Andrea Lee. Can Yealimi Noh convert from seven feet? No, she lips out!

At the par-three 11th Yealimi Noh doesn’t think much of her tee shot - and yet it settles only 8 feet from the flag. She’s not been becalmed for long.

Every match has only one hole in it. The next three hours promise to be dramatic. Europe could build a significant lead. America could pull level. And the visitors could even sneak clear ahead of the singles. It’s game on.

1UP Stark/Grant v Khang/Coughlin (12)

Woad/Hull v Noh/An. Lee 1UP (10)

Nadaud/Maguire v Zhang/Kim 1UP (9)

1UP Ciganda/Boutier v Kupcho/Duncan (8)

Turnaround at the top. Linn Grant’s approach to 12 is conceded and the birdie earns a win. The Swedes hit the 11th tee 1DOWN and they leave the 12th green 1UP.

Meanwhile Lottie Woad reduces her deficit in match two. She and Charley Hull are now only 1DOWN up against the becalmed Yealimi Noh.

If Yealimi Noh is a match play machine, Leona Maguire is a match play machine. Her Cup record reads 10-3-1 and this morning she became the fastest to 10 wins in matches played (13). The previous best was 15 by Nelly Korda and Dottie Pepper.

Maguire now makes a short birdie putt at 9 to win the hole. Added to her eagle-2 at 8, the deficit in match three is down to one hole.

Stark/Grant A/S Khang/Coughlin (11)

Woad/Hull v Noh/An. Lee 2UP (9)

Nadaud/Maguire v Zhang/Kim 1UP (9)

1UP Ciganda/Boutier v Kupcho/Duncan (8)

The top match is all square again. Linn Grant drains a 10 foot birdie putt at the par-three 11th. It’s a tremendous scrap there between two excellent and in-form combinations: Grant and Maja Stark, Lauren Coughlin and Megan Khang.

Stark told me earlier this week: “Ahead of my first Solheim Cup I had played lots of team sports and I thought I was a quiet competitor. Then all of a sudden I was playing in the Solheim Cup and I didn’t really recognise myself. I was screaming, and shouting, and reacting to every shot I hit or my partner hit. It was not just an adrenalin rush like I’ve never experienced before, it actually transformed me.

“I asked myself why it happens and I think it’s because you’re not just playing for yourself, you’re playing for the continent, your team and also for the wider LET staff because I was chatting to them earlier today and learning how hard they work all week.

“Some of them are sleeping only two or three hours a night – and they’re doing that to make our life easier this week. I’ll be thinking of them this week – and playing for them, too.”

Playing rather well for them.

Updated at 10.06 EDT

By the way, Charley Hull and Lottie Woad are the first ever Solheim Cup combination to play four sessions together. If that’s surprising, the fact they’ve only claimed half a point thus far makes it all the more so. They need to stop the Yealimi Noh birdie train to change that situation.

Yealimi Noh made 11 birdies in 16 holes to defeat Miyu Yamashita in last year’s LPGA International Crown. She has now added another birdie at 9. That’s six today and another five in her last nine holes yesterday.

She’s a match play machine.

She is now 2UP on Charley Hull and Lottie Woad. In practice, of course, Andrea Lee is also in that position. But, as yesterday, Noh is more or less playing the English pair on her own – and doing it very well.

Leona Maguire delivers a Katie Taylor combination in response to a drained pitch. A swift one-two flattens fresh air and secures the eagle-2 at the short par-four 8th – and with it the hole is won. She and Nastasia nadaud are now 2DOWN in the third match. Tremendous excitement among the many Irish in the galleries.

Eagle-2 for Yealimi Noh at 8. It’s almost getting silly how well she’s playing. At the 274-yard par-four she drove the green and then her putt tracked unerringly towards the pin, hit it, and plopped down into the cup. A far more restrained reaction from the Californian valley girl – at least in comparison with the feisty Carlota Ciganda.

Noh is now 10-under through her last 17 holes.

Carlota Ciganda, not content with draining a big winning birdie putt at 5, does it again at 6. This one is from 35 feet, and drops down a level into a bowl area of the green. It takes Europe 2UP in the final match of the day. Fist pump from the Spaniard.

Updated at 09.33 EDT

The first fourball has hit the turn. The Swedish combination of Linn Grant and Maja Stark have secured par – and Lauren Coughlin joins them to remain 1UP alongside Megan Khang.

US captain Angel Stanford received a lot of criticism for handing Khang a wildcard. Her form was undoubtedly poor, but she has yet again proved herself a transformed golfer when wearing Team USA uniform.

Stark/Grant v Khang/Coughlin 1UP (9)

Woad/Hull A/S Noh/An. Lee (7)

Nadaud/Maguire A.S Zhang/Kim 3UP (6)

1UP Ciganda/Boutier v Kupcho/Duncan (5)

Updated at 09.28 EDT

Lottie Woad drains a 10 foot birdie putt at 7 – and Yealimi Noh follows her in for the half. It’s Noh’s fourth par breaker of the day (and 10th in her last 17 holes).

Meanwhile Carlota Ciganda buries a 28 foot birdie putt at 5. It wins the hole. She and Celine Boutier move 1UP on Jennifer Kupcho and Lindy Duncan.

Rose Zhang has joined Auston Kim in making birdies in match three. A birdie at 5 sent the pair 3UP against Leona Maguire and Nastasia Nadaud. But can they make if five in a row at 6? They both have 10 feet tries but they slip past the hole.

They remain in control of that match, however.

Esther Henseleit played two magnificent chips and one outrageously good approach to help Europe win a foursomes point this morning. But her close putting was poor and she’s currently on the practice putting green doing her best to sort out her strike ahead of the singles.

Who doesn’t love a short par-four? The 274-yard 8th is a cracker and Lauren Coughlin finds the green with a terrific strike in the top match. But Linn Grant betters it, running her ball through and along the contours.

Back on 6 Charley Hull drains a winning birdie from 10 feet. She and Lottie Woad are now all square in the second match.

This is only her second match of the week but Yealimi Noh is one of the stars of this week. She was superb yesterday, pinching a half with Hull and Woad when her partner Angel Yin was all over the shop. She’s made three birdies in five holes today to take a 1UP lead with Andrea Lee over Hull and Woad (again). Sophie Walker on TV says Noh is “striping it”.

We’ve talked her up far too much, of course. At the par-three 6th she double crosses herself and finds the bunker back left. Sorry about that Yealimi.

Team USA badly need a strong comeback from a weak third session which left Europe leading 7-5.

Since 1998, teams that lead at the end of third session have an overall Solheim Cup record of 11-1-1. That’s significant. Mesnwhile, a Carlota Ciganda birdie in the bottom match has pulled that match all square.

Stark/Grant v Khang/Coughlin 1UP (6)

Woad/Hull A/S Noh/An. Lee (4)

Nadaud/Maguire v Zhang/Kim 2UP (4)

Ciganda/Boutier A/S Kupcho/Duncan (3)

Updated at 08.59 EDT

Chip in time for Auston Kim. The big hitter proves that she has touch around the green with a delicately played pitch over the edge of a bunker and across the green. Lots of noise from the American galleries and that’s two birdies in a row for Kim. She and Rose Zhang lead Leona Maguire and Nastasia Nadaud 2UP.

“The real Charley Hull has just stood up,” cried Alison Whitaker on commentary. She’s finally drained a putt, to win the 4th and bring the second match all square. A smile from the English veteran which is a welcome sight given that she’s been so introverted all week.

The pressure is on the Swedes in the top match. At the par-five 5th they both find the green in three blows and have outside chances of birdie. But the Americans Megan Khang and Lauren Coughlin are inside both of them so favourite to move further clear.

Maja Stark misses with a bold bid from 20 feet then Linn Grant makes no mistake from 10 feet. Pressure withstood. Moreover, Khang fails to match her so it’s up to Coughlin again … and she makes no mistake.

Lauren Coughlin, by the way, has become the first American to play all five sessions since Paula Creamer in 2011. This week’s host course – Bernardus – is a Kyle Phillips design and Coughlin has been a winner of the Scottish Open on his redesign as Dundonald Links.

Lauren Coughlin wins the par-three 4th with a birdie to kick clear in the top match. Then Yealimi Noh drains an 18 foot birdie putt to win the 3rd in the second game. An early advantage for Team USA and the galleries are the quietest they’ve been all day.

Stark/Grant A/S Khang/Coughlin 1UP (4)

Woad/Hull A/S Noh/An. Lee 1UP (3)

Nadaud/Maguire A.S Zhang/Kim (2)

Ciganda/Boutier v Kupcho/Duncan 1UP (1)

Can the US team edge clear on 1? Yes! Jennifer Kupcho drains a 12 foot birdie putt and they gain an early lead. On commentary Morgan Pressel approves. “That’s the first fist pump we’ve seen from Jennifer this week,” she says. There’s more than a touch of a disapproving teacher in the manner of Pressel.

Carlota Ciganda is in the last fourball out again. It’s no coincidence because she’s slow. It makes plenty of watchers … twitchy, shall we say?

Stark/Grant A/S Khang/Coughlin (3)

Woad/Hull A/S Noh/An. Lee (2)

Nadaud/Maguire A.S Zhang/Kim (1)

Ciganda/Boutier v Kupcho/Duncan

Updated at 08.07 EDT

Two chances for the Americans at 3 after both Swedes fail to make birdie. First up is Megan Khang from five feet. It slips by the hole. No mistake from Lauren Coughlin, however. The match is now all square.

Meanwhile back at the 1st tee, final action for the big crowds there as they cheer on Carlota Ciganda and Celine Boutier for Europe, and Lindy Duncan and Jennifer Kupcho for the Americans.

Updated at 07.53 EDT

Nastasia Nadaud and Leona Maguire are up against Rose Zhang and Auston Kim in the 3rd match out. None of them scaring the hole with their approach shots, however. Up ahead at 3, the American duo of Lauren Coughlin and Megan Khang are both in close with Maja Stark just outside them.

Yealimi Noh and Charley Hull set up short range birdie opportunities at the 1st, peppering the flag. It’s a duel between the pair and Hull is up first from 7 feet – but she guns it past the hole. So to Noh, who more or less took this English pair on single handedly in yesterday’s halved match (her partner Angel Yin struggled after the first few holes). She also misses, from 6 feet, so the hole is halved.

1UP Stark/Grant v Khang/Coughlin (2)

Woad/Hull v Noh/An. Lee (1)

Back on the 1st tee. Lottie Woad and Charley Hull, the misfiring English duo, are delighted when they spot team mates Esther Henseleit and Mimi Rhodes in among the singing galleries in the grandstand. It’s just about the first time Charley Hull has been smiling this week. She’s been very subdued. The obvious explanation is that she’s not A1. But there’s also a sense that she’s trying to keep everything under control and actually just inhibiting herself.

They’re up against Yealimi Noh – a star of yesterday afternoon – and Andrea Lee. Hull thrashes her ball down the fairway – can she shed those inhibitions and play to her potential?

Wow. Team USA’s Lauren Coughlin knocks her approach to kick in range at the 1st and then Europe’s Maja Stark then pops her approach in the hole on the third bounce. Sensational. What a start to the afternoon.

1UP Stark/Grant v Khang/Coughlin (1)

Updated at 07.18 EDT

It’s only the third counting score made by Lee today and the first that has won a hole. Maja Stark has drained another sensational shot. “Awesome,” cries team mate Julia Lopez Ramirez as...

articles.title: Formula One 2026: Norris pips Antonelli to Spanish Grand Prix pole by 0.011sec – live
articles.text:
1 Lando Norris 🇬🇧 McLaren 1:31.824

2 Kimi Antonelli 🇮🇹 Mercedes +0.011

3 Lewis Hamilton 🇬🇧 Ferrari +0.140

4 Max Verstappen 🇳🇱 Red Bull +0.189

5 Charles Leclerc 🇲🇨 Ferrari +0.195

6 George Russell 🇬🇧 Mercedes +0.325

7 Oscar Piastri 🇦🇺 McLaren +04.70

8 Liam Lawson 🇳🇿 Red Bull +0.492

9 Franco Colapinto 🇦🇷 Alpine +1.079

10 Arvid Lindblad 🇬🇧 Racing Bulls +1.217

David Coulthard talks to Norris: “My God, one of the best laps I’ve done ever … Pretty much everything worked perfectly.”

Updated at 11.07 EDT

1 Lando Norris 🇬🇧 McLaren 1:31.824

2 Kimi Antonelli 🇮🇹 Mercedes +0.011

3 Lewis Hamilton 🇬🇧 Ferrari +0.140

4 Max Verstappen 🇳🇱 Red Bull +0.189

5 Charles Leclerc 🇲🇨 Ferrari +0.195

6 George Russell 🇬🇧 Mercedes +0.325

7 Oscar Piastri 🇦🇺 McLaren +04.70

8 Liam Lawson 🇳🇿 Red Bull +0.492

9 Franco Colapinto 🇦🇷 Alpine +1.079

10 Arvid Lindblad 🇬🇧 Racing Bulls +1.217

The world champion, who had a poor Monza to follow his two wins, went round in 1:31.824.

Lando Norris takes pole! Mercedes lose their 100% record!

Where did that come from? Norris goes 0.011 faster than Antonelli, and for the first time this season Mercedes do not start in P1.

Updated at 11.06 EDT

Norris goes fastest!

Hamilton 0.178 behind Antonelli.

Antonelli going for it and by 0.244 goes fastest, Russell third.

This would be a great track to land that pole, and a great response to last week’s Ferrari farrago.

Lewis Hamilton has not had a pole since 2023, David Croft points out.

0.254 covers the top five: Ham, Ant, Rus, Lec, Ver.

Verstappen can only make fifth. Bernie Collins was pointing out that Ferrari have an extra set of new softs, too.

Hamilton goes fastest in 1:32.079, ahead of Antonelli and Russell!

Updated at 11.07 EDT

Norris gets a black and white flag for improper driving. Ouch.

Lando Norris gets a €900 fine for pit lane speeding.

The Mercedes duo are at the front of the Q3 queue.

Anthony Davidson shows that Gasly kissed a wall, while Bortoleto went airborne.

A morose Gasly says the car feels completely different to FP3. A big contrast from his Monza joy.

Hulkenberg, Bortoleto, Ocon, Gasly, Tsunoda and Albon, with Colapinto pulling one out to make it to Q3 again for Alpine.

Antonelli still second but only 0.034 slower than Verstappen now.

Piastri, down in eighth, has to use a new set of tyres to make sure of Q3.

Hamilton and Leclerc into the 1:32s, third and fourth.

Drop zone shaping up as Bortoleto, Tsunoda (in Lawson’s Racing Bulls), Ocon, Albon, Colapinto and Gasly.

Big escape for Franco Colapinto: he hits the ground on the showpiece La Monumental corner but keeps it together.

Verstappen goes 0.046 ahead of Antonelli, while Lawson is fourth, ahead of Norris and the Ferraris.

Updated at 10.43 EDT

Antonelli leading, 1:32.603 with Russell second +0.247.

Q2 is go. Ted Kravitz reports that Lance Stroll had a water pressure problem, while Carlos Sainz will be done for blocking Bottas.

Ollie Bearman says a gust of wind at the wrong moment did for his Haas. “I don’t feel I did much wrong. It’s a shame not to be on track because the car is fast.”

Another strong session from Liam Lawson. After last year’s rapid demotion, he now looks the part as a temporary Red Bull driver.

George Russell goes fastest! What a mixed session for him: kissed a wall, is being investigated for not following race director orders, but his 1:33.211 is ahead of Antonelli by 0.056.

Out go Sainz, Alonso, Perez, Bottas, Bearman and Stroll.

The pain in Spain: Sainz and Alonso both going out.

Lindblad, shaken up by the crash, was at risk, but pulls out a lap.

But Antonelli now goes quickest, 0.043 faster than Lawson.

Very tight at the top: Russell in seventh is only 0.278 behind Lawson.

Drop zone is now Alonso, Albon, Perez, Bottas, Stroll and the absent Bearman.

Lawson still fastest, but ahead of his fellow Red Bull Verstappen by only 0.065 now.

Russell kisses the wall but keeps it together and is up to sixth, 0.278.

Ocon has escaped the drop zone at Alonso’s expense.

Antonelli had a lock-up and ran off the track but there was space to stop.

The drop zone is Perez, Bottas, Lindblad, Stroll and Albon, plus the absent Bearman.

Norris is running fourth, ahead of Bortoleto.

Pierre Gasly, last week’s pole sitter, is down in 12th.

Liam Lawson, again in the Red Bull with Isack Hadjar injured, goes fastest. 1:33.316.

Verstappen 0.178 back, with Leclerc and Hamilton also going faster than Russell … and so does Bortoleto, beating the Ferraris!

Antonelli looking good. 1:33.566; Russell 1:34.376. Ouch for the Briton.

Updated at 10.10 EDT

And off we go for Q1. A proper queue, everyone keen to be out early on a new circuit.

Do F1 fans in Barcelona object to the fact that they have lost the Spanish GP to Madrid, or are they pleased they now get the Catalunya GP? Probably both.

But Bearman’s picture could have been left out. New chassis needed, no can drive.

Portentous countdown time.

Bernie Collins predicts Kimi Antonelli will take pole. “Surprise, surprise,” says the ever-hoarse Simon Lazenby.

Oliver Bearman may not make qualifying. Ted Kravitz says things are not looking good for the Haas after his FP3 crash.

And here are the constructors:

1 Mercedes 🇩🇪 468pts

5 Racing Bulls 🇮🇹 75

10 Aston Martin 🇬🇧 3

A reminder of how the drivers stand after the Italian Grand Prix (and Pierre Gasly’s loss of his third place in Monaco):

1 Kimi Antonelli 🇮🇹 Mercedes 267pts

2 George Russell 🇬🇧 Mercedes 201

3 Lewis Hamilton 🇬🇧 Ferrari 191

4 Lando Norris 🇬🇧 McLaren 171

5 Charles Leclerc 🇲🇨 Ferrari 155

6 Max Verstappen 🇳🇱 Red Bull 127

7 Oscar Piastri 🇦🇺 McLaren 116

8 Isack Hadjar 🇫🇷 Red Bull 71

9 Liam Lawson 🇳🇿 Racing Bulls 51

10 Pierre Gasly 🇫🇷 Alpine 41

11 Arvid Lindblad 🇬🇧 Racing Bulls 29

12 Franco Colapinto 🇦🇷 Alpine 21

13 Oliver Bearman 🇬🇧 Haas 18

14 Gabriel Bortoleto 🇧🇷 Audi 10

15 Nico Hülkenberg 🇩🇪 Audi 6

16 Carlos Sainz 🇪🇸 Williams 6

17 Alexander Albon 🇹🇭 Williams 5

18 Esteban Ocon 🇫🇷 Haas 3

19 Fernando Alonso 🇪🇸 Aston Martin 3

20 Yuki Tsunoda 🇯🇵 Racing Bulls 1

Lance Stroll 🇨🇦 Aston Martin

Valtteri Bottas 🇫🇮 Cadillac

Sergio Pérez 🇲🇽 Cadillac

Martin Brundle has been talking to George Russell about Monza, and the decision not to pit when Antonelli did. Russell says he thought it was the right decision at the time, and pays honest tribute to his remarkable teammate: “He is doing an amazing job … the truth is he is faster than me at the moment … You just have to take your hat off.”

Updated at 09.39 EDT

It was a similar story in FP3 for Antonelli:

double quotation markLewis Hamilton crashed his Ferrari in final practice for the Spanish ⁠Grand Prix at Madrid’s new Formula One circuit on Saturday, halting the session with just over half an hour left, while Mercedes’ ⁠championship leader Kimi Antonelli ⁠was fastest …

The session was red-flagged and the clock then temporarily stopped for barrier repairs with 15 minutes to go. When it restarted, Antonelli knocked Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc off the top of the timesheets with a time of 1min and ‌32.797sec, 0.166 quicker than the Monegasque …

Haas’s Oliver Bearman then brought out ​the red flags again in the final minute when he spun and hit the barriers backwards at turn 11, the approach to La Monumental, the circuit’s banked signature curve.

double quotation markMcLaren’s Oscar Piastri was third quickest ahead of his teammate Lando Norris, with Red Bull’s Max Verstappen fifth and ⁠Russell sixth.

Red Bull’s Liam Lawson and Audi’s Nico Hülkenberg were seventh and ​eighth, with Hamilton ninth and ​Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto completing the top ​10.

Qualifying followed two hours later and will be crucial for Sunday’s race, ​with overtaking likely ‌to be difficult on ​a challenging layout ​that Russell said on Friday had less margin for error than Monaco because of the close walls but higher speeds involved.

Toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, said: “Nobody really knows what to expect. The session was tight. It’s about putting a lap together without mistakes and traffic.” Reuters

Right, half an hour to go till qualifying. Lewis Hamilton and Oliver Bearman were not the first to crash in F1 practice. Though Friday’s first session passed off quietly, Arvid Lindblad went off in FP2 … while Antonelli went serenely on:

double quotation markKimi Antonelli lapped fastest for Mercedes in free practice at Madrid’s new Spanish Grand Prix circuit on Friday, with Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton ⁠close behind.

Second in a first ⁠practice led by teammate George ​Russell, Antonelli then set the pace in a later session halted briefly by Racing Bulls’ British rookie Arvid Lindblad becoming the first F1 driver to crash at the Madring and bring out red flags.

“It ⁠is a very cool circuit to drive around. It is a real challenge for us as drivers, with lots of high-speed corners and walls close by,” said Antonelli.

double quotation markAntonelli’s best lap of 1min 33.662sec was 0.113 quicker ⁠than Leclerc’s fastest effort. Hamilton was 0.149 off the pace with Lindblad fourth despite the crash ending his session with 24 minutes to go.

The ​19-year-old lost control of the rear of the car and smashed ‌into the barriers sideways at turn 13.

“It ‌looked quite bad from the outside, but thankfully the impact wasn’t too heavy and I feel completely fine. There’s some damage to the car, ‌so I apologise to the team for the extra work they’ll have to do tonight,” said Lindblad. Reuters

There were suggestions Hamilton might face a penalty for trying to drive back to the pits with a damaged car but Sky F1 reports he is in the clear.

Kimi Antonelli does not need luck. Last year his promotion to the second seat at Mercedes looked premature and he was exposed on occasion, but he thoroughly absorbed every lesson and is a deserved leader of the title race. But fortune has favoured him too, whether indirectly – such as the catalogue of agonies suffered by his teammate George Russell, who would otherwise be far closer in the standings than 66 points – or directly, as was the case with a red flag and a virtual safety car in last Sunday’s Italian Grand Prix, which enabled him to turn 19th place on the grid into a win.

Antonelli does not hesitate to credit Toto Wolff and the rest of the Mercedes team, not just for producing the car. The biggest decision was promoting an 18-year-old into the seat for last season, but even in smaller ones they have been vindicated, such as choosing Monza, with its openings for overtaking, as the venue for Antonelli to take the penalties for utilising new power unit components.

But with Antonelli winning in such unpropitious circumstances, the title race – which looked as if it could open up after Lando Norris’s back-to-back wins – could soon be a procession. Maybe what F1 needs right now is a new track to spice things up.

Enter the Madring, which may or may not prove an unfortunate bit of nominative determinism. As Giles Richards reports, Russell described the circuit as “mental” after watching Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak crash in F2 practice:

double quotation markRussell observed the Madring was set to be an even sterner test than Monaco. “I would put this as a circuit that has less margin, purely because of the speed,” he said. “In Monaco the walls are closer but because you’re going slower – if you make a mistake you’re not into the wall as quickly, and you can recover it sometimes. It’s more lock-up. Here, there’s less margin.”

The issue, explained Russell, was that the fast corners were combined with the angles of the barriers on exit. “You see at this barrier, it’s kind of like coming back on to the track,” he said, indicating where the smoking wreckage of Inthraphuvasak’s car was sitting. “So if you are to go wide and hit the wall, you’re not hitting it at the same angle as the car is going. The car is going towards the wall but the wall is sort of coming in.”

Oliver Bearman certainly found it testing in Saturday’s FP3, and so did Lewis Hamilton:

double quotation markLewis Hamilton crashed his Ferrari in final practice for the ⁠Spanish Grand Prix at Madrid’s new Formula One circuit on Saturday, bringing the ⁠session to a ⁠halt ​with just over half an hour remaining.

The seven-times world champion locked up and went ⁠into the barriers at the final corner. He managed to reverse out and tried to get ⁠the damaged Ferrari back to the Madring pitlane, virtually ​a whole lap, while ‌ignoring team instructions ‌to stop.

The Briton eventually did pull over, with the front ‌wing still wedged under the car which also had a punctured front right tyre.

“Stop the car. Stop in the safest place possible,” he had been told earlier.

“If I can make it back I will. If ‌not, I will do it safely,” replied Hamilton, who returned to the pits on the back ​of a moped after parking up. Press Association

A hybrid of streets and purpose-built sections, Madrid’s new circuit is certainly a challenge. Join me from 2.30pm BST in the buildup to the 3pm start to Spanish Grand Prix qualifying, and in the meantime here’s Giles’s full on-the-ground look at the Madring.

articles.title: PlayStation gambles with 18-rated Wolverine game - does it pay off?
articles.text:
On Tuesday, Sony will release Marvel's Wolverine - the biggest game exclusive to the PlayStation 5 this year.

It's made by Insomniac, the studio responsible for the recent Spider-Man titles, which have sold 50 million copies in recent years.

But unlike the friendly neighbourhood superhero, Wolverine has a Pegi-18 rating in the UK, meaning a child cannot legally buy the game, and it contains considerable levels of blood, gore and violence.

It represents a gamble for the studio responsible for some of Sony's biggest hits - will it turn out to have been worth it?

This review does not reveal the game's biggest moments, but beware minor spoilers for some of the characters that appear and a few early sequences. Some of the images contain blood.

There are some stealth options, but I generally ignored them and went in with my claws out. The game didn't penalise me for this.

You also unlock a slew of abilities, much like other games in the genre, meaning you get even more powerful as the game rumbles on.

And a clever system allows you to spend the rage you have accumulated to regenerate your health.

The combat kept me hooked the whole way through the game, which took about 20 hours to get to the end credits. My colleague was faster, clocking in at about 15 hours.

When Spider-Man released in 2018, it set a new standard for superhero games with an open-world New York City which you could freely (and entertainingly) explore by web-slinging through the skies.

It was so influential that it spawned a popular online gag, pointing fun at reviewers who couldn't help but repeat a cliché, external about the game making them feel like Spider-Man.

"There's a significant shake-up happening here in game design terms," freelance game critic Emma Kent told me.

"Insomniac is moving away from Spider-Man's open world formula to adopt a linear structure for Wolverine.

"That means less open exploration, and a more curated path through the game world."

It adds to the gamble that comes with the game having such graphic violence.

"Peter Parker and Miles Morales would go out of their way to avoid killing enemies - stringing them up or gluing them against walls with his webs - and there was no real gore to speak of," Kent said.

"Some games truly revel in showing detailed and over-exaggerated gore, but the violence in Marvel's Wolverine doesn't feel particularly gratuitous.

"When you build up a sense of flow, it really does feel like you're rampaging through dozens of enemies, and I think the blood splashes are an important way of displaying the carnage you're causing."

The reality is by having a higher age rating than Spider-Man, it is by definition reducing the amount of people who can buy the game. And the game's director Mike Daly accepted this came with a risk.

"Even though this character appeals to kids, making a game that is explicitly like, 'sorry, this is not for kids, you should not play this game' - it does reduce the scope," he said.

"But I think there was no other way to do it. That was the cost of doing business if we really wanted to set a game with this character in this universe."

One thing I didn't expect was the game's reliance on its performers.

Gameplay is frequently interrupted with cutscenes, which will I'm sure prove divisive.

Nonetheless, the acting is top drawer, with the standout being veteran performer Troy Baker (known for many roles including Joel in The Last of Us) who puts in a memorable performance as Nathaniel Essex.

Liam McIntyre, who plays Wolverine, told BBC Newsbeat he was "looking forward to people playing it".

"I'm so proud that people are resonating with the story, with the performances, the character," he said.

"This is such an astoundingly good character piece.

"I'm so happy that I've been able to make a Wolverine that hopefully people love."

And to that point - when Hugh Jackman's famous take on the character last appeared on the big screen in 2024's Deadpool & Wolverine, it made $205m (then £160m) on opening weekend in the US - the best ever opening for an R-rated film.

It all suggests Sony's gamble may be a safer bet than it first seems.

I'll avoid discussing the story so as not to spoil it, but suffice to say I was engaged, even if at times I felt I was spending too long watching videos and not enough time using the controller.

Clearly the developers were inspired by narrative adventures like Uncharted for this kind of storytelling, and the gameplay even feels similar at times with chase and climbing sequences.

And while that game was genre-defining, it came out almost 20 years ago, so it's hardly a favourable comparison.

In fact, perhaps the biggest issue for Wolverine is that it doesn't reinvent the wheel like Spider-Man did.

It's a game packed with tight combat and excellent performances, but it never threatens to meet the genre-defining heights of Insomniac's previous offering.

And Daly said there was a "monumental" amount of pressure that came with making the game following the success of Spider-Man - but as to whether the gamble paid off, he took a Zen view.

"I measure success when I hear people talk to me about the game, who are Wolverine fans, and they say 'thank you for making this, you nailed it'," he said.

"If I hear that, it's like, yes, we did it. That's what we set out to do."

articles.title: Why brazen museum thefts keep happening nearly a year after Louvre heist
articles.text:
When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir, worth millions of euros, not everyone was surprised.

Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen.

And just days before the Renoir heist, internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely - particularly in the wake of the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October.

The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on.

"We will see more of this," says Brand, "because if you are able to hit the Louvre, thieves all around the world are watching that, thinking, 'Wow' - and then they think, 'Don't we have a local museum with gold and silver?'".

Within hours of the Louvre burglary, thieves had raided coins from a smaller museum in France. Since then, criminals have stolen a diamond necklace in Vienna, Bronze Age artefacts in Spain, and art from two Italian museums - and that's only what the BBC has written about.

The heist at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer is the latest, and detectives are still working to track down the remaining multi-million-pound paintings - two of which were quickly recovered after thieves dropped them in the museum garden.

Europol tells the BBC the number of museum theft cases reported to them across Europe began to increase about two years ago.

Its recent report says both the methods and targets of thefts are changing - with a rise in more forceful tactics, and, as in the Louvre case, a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones.

Both Brand and Ibrahim Bulut, a museum security expert from a Belgian security consulting firm, believe many thefts that followed the Louvre burglary are copycats.

"Every museum in the world is stressing now," Brand says. "In every museum there have been meetings with the security officer or with the police."

Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared with well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash.

Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds.

For example, the Denis Diderot Maison des Lumières (House of Enlightenment) - burgled hours after the Louvre - is housed in two 18th-Century mansions in Langres.

"We therefore have to reconcile modern security requirements with the need to preserve historic buildings and comply with France's heritage regulations," local mayor Théo Caviezel explains.

Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe.

And even if a museum is secured well, thieves could still come in armed, Brand says, adding that it would be impractical to put police in galleries.

Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes.

Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month, external points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside.

In the Louvre, the thieves used a mechanical lift to gain access, cut through the window with power tools and then threatened guards, who left, before forcing their way inside displays and grabbing the jewels. In the Renoir case, the perpetrators used an electric knife to cut through a fence before sawing through structures holding the paintings' frames in place.

The increased aggression creates new security concerns.

"An armed incident during opening hours, like the one we experienced, creates a situation in which the immediate priority is to keep our audience and staff safe," says Lilli Hollein, the director of the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna, which was burgled last month.

What is being stolen is also changing. While paintings are still taken, they're harder to sell, so about 10 years ago, thieves began shifting to goods that are easier to get rid of, Brand says.

Now precious metals, gemstones, and culturally significant artefacts including Chinese porcelain are increasingly targeted, according to Europol's report.

"Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process," it says. "Precious stones in jewellery, on the other hand, can be easily removed and sold further."

Meanwhile, Chinese porcelain is likely to be easily sold on the art market because of high demand, Europol says.

After a theft, police generally have between four and six days to catch the thieves, according to Brand, who works with investigators by calling informants and receiving tips from the public or even ex-partners of perpetrators.

But while suspects may be arrested, jewels or precious metals might not be found - such as with the Louvre case.

On the other hand, Brand believes the Renoir paintings stolen this week - two of which were dropped by the thieves on their way out - "will probably be recovered" because "no one will want to buy" them and "it is likely, then, that the thieves have no idea what to do with them".

Christopher A Marinello, the boss of Art Recovery International that recovers stolen art, says only 5-10% of stolen art is ever recovered, making thefts from small museums like this week's "extra painful".

Tuesday's heist is another example of "Europe's museums under siege", he adds.

After its theft in October, Maison des Lumières launched a security audit carried out by police officers appointed by France's cultural ministry, mayor Caviezel says.

Some recommendations are already being implemented, such as enhanced video surveillance, while other structural improvements are in the process of being developed.

MAK in Vienna also increased its security to prevent "copycat offenders and to provide our audience with visible security", its director says. Entry is through a metal detector, and bags must be put in the cloakroom or in lockers, and there are more security guards.

Experts say the trick is to create physical barriers that will delay thieves so there is time for the police to arrive, or to make any theft take so long that it would deter would-be offenders from attempting it.

"Security is about buying time", says Bulut. "The objective is not to make the theft theoretically impossible, but to make removal difficult, noisy, detectable and above all, time-consuming, because to be very honest, thefts can always happen, it's the timing that you're concerned about."

Brand says a delay could be building an extra, heavy door anchored into the ground, thickening the glass on display cases or using a fog machine.

Sokka says it's critical to have integrated systems - so for example if an alarm goes off, you could shut down the facility, or lock down all high net worth paintings.

However, security measures are expensive. Mayor Caviezel, whose small French city hosts two museums and collections, says finding the money is "one of our main challenges".

"A small city can be entrusted with collections of national importance without having the financial resources of a major Parisian institution."

Bulut, who sits on the International Committee for Museum Security board, says it's not all about expensive gadgets. It could also be training guards to spot suspicious people who may be casing a museum and ask them if they need help, which may deter them from returning.

Museums are investing: Sokka says his company has seen an uptick in seismic offerings, that can detect vibration such as drilling in walls, in the past 18 months.

Museum heists are not increasing everywhere in Europe. In Sweden, major museum thefts began to decline around a decade ago and have not changed significantly in recent years, said Peg Magnusson, Sweden's representative for a Unesco convention to combat illicit trafficking of cultural property. However, other worrying cultural artefact targets have emerged.

The challenge for museums now is increasing security while also staying open to the public.

"A museum cannot be a fortress," Hollein says. "We want to be open institutions; at the same time, we are facing new challenges and attacks against museums that will require new standards."

articles.title: UK economy sees surprise growth in July helped by AI boom
articles.text:
The UK's economy grew faster than expected in July partly helped by businesses using artificial intelligence (AI).

The economy expanded by 0.4%, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, whereas analysts had predicted no growth.

Growth in July was helped by a strong performance from the services sector, and particularly computer programming.

Experts said the figure showed the UK economy was proving resilient in the face of shocks such as the war in Iran, but they expect growth to slow in the months ahead as high energy prices affect households.

July's figure follows growth of 0.3% in June and zero growth in May.

According to the ONS director of economic statistics, Liz McKeown, there was evidence that businesses involved with AI and related technologies helped to boost the sector, not just in July but in May and June as well.

The ONS said many of the IT businesses reporting the largest turnover "appear to be involved with AI", though it said it is difficult to quantify the exact impact of AI.

McKeown also said some businesses had said that the warm weather and football world cup had affected activity in July, although she said the effects "differed across industries, benefitting some businesses while creating challenges for others".

The ONS said that in the three months to July, which gives a better underlying picture, the economy grew by 0.4% compared with the previous three months.

Rob Arnold, co-founder of Ascendea, an AI firm which employs nine people, believes the UK hasn't seen the real economic growth potential from the technology yet.

He says his company is able to develop apps for other businesses "100 times quicker at a 50th of the cost" because of AI, but that the UK government needs to do more to invest in the sector as there are currently better opportunities in the US.

He knows a few small UK-based AI firms that have either moved to the US or are thinking of doing so due to a lack of UK government support.

Alongside grants and funding, he says the government also needs to invest in training companies on how to use AI as it can be dangerous if not understood properly. "It's like playing with a weapon," he says.

Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said July's data showed "the resilience of the economy in the first half of the year continued into the second half".

However, he added that higher energy prices and borrowing costs would soon start to hit growth, especially if the rises seen this week are sustained.

The Iran war has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices - affecting households and businesses.

This rise in energy costs has led to fears that inflation will remain high, and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep price rises under control.

The Bank of England is meeting next week to discuss interest rates. Economists widely expect rates to be held, but some have predicted an increase before the end of the year.

Chancellor John Healey said the economy, was "demonstrating a welcome resilience, despite serious global uncertainty".

"Our growth although still fragile was the fastest in the G7 in the first half of the year," he added.

"But, the conflict in the Middle East does have impacts here at home - from the cost of the weekly family shop to the cost of government borrowing."

Healey is to present his first Budget in October. He told BBC News this week that he wants people to confident about the economy, despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said nobody in the government "should be high-fiving themselves" over the latest figures.

"Our construction and production sectors are shrinking, unemployment is up under Labour, and we've got the highest government borrowing rates in almost 30 years."
