articles.title: Man to Man review – Tilda Swinton’s perfect pacing makes this multi-character monologue compelling
articles.text:
Early autumn London theatre has already featured two Oscar winners: Cate Blanchett in Electra/Persona and Mark Rylance in Tartuffe (Remixed). Now Tilda Swinton makes a trio. This shows the commendable dedication of some screen talent to theatre but also the box office need, in recessions, for famous faces. Unusually, there was a first night red carpet outside the Royal Court, leading a writer long associated with the venue to express “shock” to ushers at such Hollywood vulgarity.

Swinton is reprising Manfred Karge’s Man to Man, which she first performed 39 years ago, in a production heading to Edinburgh, Berlin and New York. The piece is a multicharacter monologue starting in Germany in the 1930s.

When her husband, Max, dies, Ella Gericke puts on his clothes and takes over his job as a crane operator. She seems to act from some combination of bereavement denial, cross-gender curiosity and proto-feminist belief in equal employment.

Ella’s challenge as Max is to be a bloke unremarkable enough not to alert men or arouse women. The next worst thing that could happen is Germany calling up men to war with the resulting medicals and barrack rooms.

In the most chilling moment, the workmates’ certainty of her masculinity becomes dangerous when the lads attempt debagging to seek evidence of circumcision that might then have led to death.

With high hair and white body paint that may suggest disguise or scabies, Swinton strikingly resembles David Bowie’s avatar Aladdin Sane, an earlier project exploring androgyny. With a gruff laddishness as her base tone, Swinton – on a Bunny Christie set dotted with period East German technology including fridge and tape machine – regularly transforms verbally and physically into other women and men.

When the play premiered, identity fluidity was largely a metaphor or aspiration rather than the reality it now is, giving the text another level. The framing has also changed politically. Man to Man had 26 scenes when premiered in Germany in 1982 and first performed by Swinton five years later.

Karge’s new section, featuring the fall of the Berlin Wall, featured in a 2015 Edinburgh fringe revival the dramatist has now written a 28th, addressing the renaissance of Nazi ideology in Germany: “The war dead have risen / In the dark of night.” There is a stinging topicality in this coda being premiered just five days after the far-right AfD party topped the state polls in Saxony-Anhalt. The 88-year-old playwright’s continuing revisions emphasise that the ghosts of 1930s Germany still walk almost a century on.

Anthony Vivis’s 1980s English version, revised by director Stephen Unwin, conveys Karge’s knack for vivid imagery. A smoker’s yellow-stained finger is able to write an endearment in after-sex sweat on Ella’s body; Hitler youth piss swastikas in the snow.

The show at times resembles performance art – Swinton slept in a glass box as a living exhibit in a 1995 installation – but the performer’s verbal flexibility and perfect pacing make Man To Man compelling theatre. However incongruously at an historically radical venue, this truly is a red carpet event.

articles.title: From Practical Magic 2 to Saturday Night Live UK: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead
articles.text:
The beloved fantasy romance from the 1990s returns with Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman reprising their roles as the Owens sisters. The story picks up 25 years later, with more family secrets and curses in the offing, plus a trip to the UK. Sure to be spellbinding stuff.

Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?

Out 18 September for one night only

Captured during their 2025 tour, this music documentary blends footage from the live shows with archive material and new narration from Jarvis Cocker, to trace the band’s rise from outsider status in Sheffield to global fame, via megahits such as Common People and lesser-known fan favourites. Directed by Garth Jennings.

Andrew Scott heads up an all-star cast in a drama exploring the second world war from a slightly quirky angle: the weather forecast. Don’t laugh: it was a crucial piece of the puzzle in the 72 hours leading up to D-day, with Britain’s chief meteorological officer James Stagg unexpectedly finding himself the man of the moment.

Everybody Digs Bill Evans

A winner at the Berlin festival, Grant Gee’s biopic explores the aftermath of the death of bass player Scott LaFaro, and the impact the tragedy has on jazz pianist Bill Evans, who is torn between New York and suburbia as he attempts to navigate his profound grief. Starring Anders Danielsen Lie, Bill Pullman and Laurie Metcalf. Catherine Bray

Birmingham, 12 September; Manchester, 15 September; Bristol, 16 September; London, 18 September; tour continues to 26 September

The beloved indie dance-pop trio head out on their final tour after more than 30 years. So expect songs such as the bangersome Glad from last year’s album International to rub shoulders with their 90s classics. Michael Cragg

Symphony Hall, Birmingham, 17 September

The dynamic Japanese conductor has embarked on one of classical music’s great endurance tests: a complete cycle of Gustav Mahler’s symphonies. Symphony No 2 promises to be a truly monumental season-opener – and also marks the CBSO Chorus’s 1,000th performance. Flora Willson

London, 15 September; Leeds, 16 September; Aberdeen, 17 September; Cambridge, 18 September

The album Dear Paul by this versatile saxophonist was dedicated to Paul Motian, his old employer and one of jazz’s most creative percussionists. These gigs with fine Swiss drummer Florian Arbenz, a true Motian inheritor, will confirm just why. John Fordham

Dublin, 15 September; London, 17 September; Brighton, 18 September

Released in April, A Wave That Will Never Break marked the return of the enigmatic Manchester experimentalists after their 2012 split. It luxuriates in what they call “heavy pop” so remember your earplugs. MC

Irving Gallery, Oxford, to 10 October

This north Devon-based artist is seriously into recycling, taking discarded old clothes, breaking them down and turning them into a mouldable, papier mache-style pulp and twisting them into wobbly geometric shapes.

Camden Art Centre, London, to 17 January

It’s the debut UK institutional show by this influential American sculptor and ceramicist, filled with rocky, prehistoric-looking references to cosmic matter, ancient mythology and the grizzly politics of resource extraction.

White Cube Bermondsey, London, 16 September to 8 November

Mexico’s leading conceptualist returns to London for another show of minimal, ephemeral geometric installation work, this time dealing with the idea that objects can act as historical records.

Celebrating Julia Carter Preston, Ceramicist

Various venues, Liverpool, to 28 February

Liverpool is rolling out the red carpet for home-town ceramics hero Julia Carter Preston (1926-2012) with five galleries across the city hosting displays of her work at the same time, including shows at the Bluecoat and Walker Art Gallery. Eddy Frankel

Stockton, 12 September; Leeds, 13 September; Tunbridge Wells, 16 September; Northampton, 17 September; Guildford, 18 September; touring to 23 May

Thanks to hit podcasts, presenting gigs and film cameos, a small cohort of millennial standups have finally ascended to the mainstream comedy firmament. Foremost among them is 36-year-old Wang, who returns to muse on ageing and his generation in new show Uh Oh. Rachel Aroesti

Jasmin Vardimon: Lullaby

JV Home, Ashford, 18 & 19 September; touring to 13 February

The work that got choreographer Jasmin Vardimon noticed 23 years ago was a dance-theatre piece called Lullaby, set on a hospital ward. Two decades later, she’s revisiting and reinventing it for today’s world. Lyndsey Winship

Almeida theatre, London, to 31 October

Director Sam Yates has assembled a knockout cast for his revival of Clifford Odets’s classic American play. Josh O’Connor stars as a gifted violinist, drawn into the brutal world of professional boxing in depression-era New York. Miriam Gillinson

Till The Stars Come Down

Nottingham Playhouse, to 26 September

Beth Steel’s heartfelt and exquisitely observed comedy was an Olivier-nominated smash in the West End. It’s set in Mansfield, where a family gather for a wedding. MG

Staying in: Streaming

Prime Video, 16 September

The Alan Ritchson-led TV adaptation of Lee Child’s Jack Reacher novels has been a huge hit with critics and viewers, making a spin-off a no-brainer. This new series revolves around Maria Sten’s titular protege and private investigator.

Saturday Night Live UK

Sky One & Now, 12 September, 10pm

A new prime minister means plenty of fresh material for the British iteration of the US sketch behemoth, but let’s hope the show doesn’t change too drastically: series one’s subtle edginess and stubborn idiosyncrasy was a recipe for surprising, naysayer-silencing success.

Channel 4, 13 September, 9pm

Channel 4 be Channel 4-ing with its latest discomfiting social experiment. A group of civilians are left in an abandoned town to test how they cope with the kind of end-of-civilisation situation (no running water, no heating, no electricity) that could in reality be merely a couple of cyber-attacks away.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story

Netflix, 17 September

Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan’s queasily contentious anthology series has previously dramatised the lives of some of America’s most notorious killers. This time round, however, the focus is on a more ambiguous figure in Borden, who was ultimately acquitted of the 1892 murders of her father and stepmother. RA

Marvel’s Wolverine

PS5; out 15 September

The creators of the brilliant Marvel’s Spider-Man games take on an altogether more brutal hero in this pummelling slash-’em-up. Evil billionaire Bolivar Trask is kidnapping mutants and only you and your claws can stop him.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave

Nintendo Switch 2; out 17 September

In the vast, fantastical Dagdan empire, warriors gather to fight in a tournament where the winner is granted one wish – but dark forces are gathering on the horizon and the fate of young contender Cai is in your hands. Expect an epic narrative adventure with fiendish tactical combat. Keith Stuart

Staying in: Albums

Bloc Party – Anatomy of a Brief Romance

Following a further lineup reshuffle in 2023 – new bassist Harry Deacon makes his debut here – art-rockers Bloc Party return with their seventh album. Produced by Trevor Horn, songs such as Love Bombs and Coming on Strong are full of frontman Kele Okereke’s tightly wound energy.

This Is Lorelei – The Singer in My Band

As one half of art-rock misfits Water from Your Eyes, Nate Amos, AKA This Is Lorelei, often deals in shape-shifting abstraction. On The Singer in My Band, however, he swaps that for twangy guitar riffs, crumpled Elliott Smith-esque singalongs and a surprising amount of sunshine.

Standing on the Corner – II

Formed in Brooklyn more than a decade ago, Standing on the Corner, who have previously worked with Solange, are a multidisciplinary collective led by Gio Escobar. On the frazzled II they blend psychedelia, rock, no-wave rap, R&B and post-hardcore into a heavy sonic soup.

Sylvan Esso – Ow ∞

Having built their own studio, the American electropop duo of Amelia Randall Meath and Nick Sanborn set about improvising, writing five to 10 songs a day. The result is this obscurely titled fifth album, which features the pogoing Hot Slob and the blown-out bop Sledge. MC

Staying in:Brain food

Across the Horizon

Musician Bob Holmes hosts this soothing series analysing the world of ambient country music. He and his guests, including guitarist Hayden Pedigo, discuss how Americana can conjure imaginative worlds.

YouTuber and linguist RobWords produces fascinating video essays on the many quirks of the English language. Highlights include the hidden logic behind typographical symbols, the literal meanings of body parts and sarcastic punctuation.

The story picks up 25 years later, with more family secrets and curses in the offing, plus a trip to the UK. Sure to be spellbinding stuff. Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? Out 18...

articles.title: Last Seen to Angine de Poitrine: the week in rave reviews
articles.text:
If you only watch one, make it …

Apple TV; available now

Summed up in a sentence In this gripping Australian thriller, emergency call handler Ian (Patrick Brammall, fresh from Colin from Accounts) thinks his missing daughter is still alive after he takes a mysterious call.

What our reviewer said “It doesn’t just pile on the twists; it makes the twists really matter, because we always understand, with painful clarity, the emotional consequences for the people experiencing them. This is riveting television, and one of the standout shows of the year.” Luke Buckmaster

Read the full review

Colin from Accounts

BBC iPlayer; available now

Summed up in a sentence The final season of the charming hit Aussie romcom picks up three years after Ashley rejected Gordon’s humiliating proposal.

What our reviewer said “Colin from Accounts has been like a ray of sunshine in the schedules. It’s been a huge hit across the world, and many will mourn its ending. I hope it turns out to be a happy one at least.” Rachel Aroesti

Read the full review

Britain’s Forgotten Girls

BBC iPlayer; available now

Summed up in a sentence An infuriating look at how victims of grooming gangs in the UK have been repeatedly failed by authorities.

What our reviewer said “The details are few and horrifying. A number of them mention having to go to school as if nothing had happened the night after an inaugural gang-rape. Your mind can hardly take it in.” Lucy Mangan

Read the full review

Tommy Robinson: Where’s the Money Gone?

Channel 4; available now

Summed up in a sentence Matt Shea investigates a number of allegations about the co-founder of the English Defence League’s finances – and puts big questions to him.

What our reviewer said “Has Shea landed an unanswerable haymaker? Not quite. Would any evidence of impropriety cause the flow of money from the faithful to dry up? Probably not. But this programme asks a lot of the right awkward questions.” Jack Seale

Read the full review

You may have missed …

ITV1; available now

Summed up in a sentence Neil Forsyth’s excellent Leith-set dark comedy drama Guilt relocates to Fremantle, Perth, where a brother and sister accidentally kill someone.

What our reviewer said “Reckless is a fantastic, fun ride grounded by a realistically fractious, but at heart loving, relationship between the siblings, the light but piercing commentary on the wider racial and socioeconomic dynamics at work in Australia, and a cast of credible, however idiosyncratic, characters whose size makes the tonal consistency all the more wildly impressive.” Lucy Mangan

Read the full review

If you only watch one, make it …

Everybody Digs Bill Evans

Summed up in a sentence Grant Gee’s film delves into the creative and personal torment of the great American jazz pianist – with a terrific supporting Bill Pullman turn as his cantankerous father.

What our reviewer said “It’s a film about music; particularly, about what remains when a musician cannot play and is left to consider the terrible sacrifices made, without conscious consent, to this all-consuming vocation that creates family pain and jealousy almost as a toxic byproduct.” Peter Bradshaw

Read the full review

Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger

Summed up in a sentence The Gallagher brothers’ mammoth comeback concerts are given the full fan-worship treatment, but it’s impossible to begrudge the euphoria they have created.

What our reviewer said “We see again the Oasis congregation engaging in colossal Dionysian events of mass joy – but of course, the poignancy of time passing and the irresistible narrative of the brothers’ public reconciliation give a new layer of emotion to the songs.” Peter Bradshaw

Read the full review

Further reading ‘Would they fight or hug?’ The Oasis comeback film’s makers on shooting fans, vicars, police – and the Gallaghers

Better Go Mad in the Wild

Summed up in a sentence Director Miro Remo journeys deep into the Czech countryside to find two brothers living an isolated life filled with quixotic ideas in this surreal documentary.

What our reviewer said “There is copious wisdom regarding family, nature, interdependency and love in this rowdy, rapturous and brilliant film.” Phil Hoad

Read the full review

Summed up in a sentence Claude Chabrol’s eerie 1969 domestic thriller charts a complex marriage in which a husband suspects his wife is cheating on him.

What our reviewer said “It does not in fact look like a classic noir thriller in the style of Chabrol’s hero Hitchcock, which is how it is often described, but more like something by Buñuel: an elaborate absurdist joke at the expense of the French bourgeoisie, a ballet of repression and fear.” Peter Bradshaw

Read the full review

Call My Agent! The Movie

Netflix; available 10 September

Summed up in a sentence The gang get back together for a spin-off of the French talent-agency sitcom, with Andréa and Noémie at the heart of chaotic events.

What our reviewer said “Writers Fanny Herrero, Lison Daniel and Violaine Bellet, along with director Émilie Noblet, skilfully open the tap and let the stream of industry-insider jokes flow at an even pace but make sure that the final product never feels smug, sentimental or self-congratulatory.” Leslie Felperin

Read the full review

Further reading Call My Agent!’s Camille Cottin on becoming a sex symbol in her 40s: ‘There’s a desire to see women who’ve been invisible’

If you only read one, make it …

Hawking by Graham Farmelo

Reviewed by Philip Ball

Summed up in a sentence An unflinching biography of the celebrated physicist.

What our reviewer said “The unavoidable truth is that Hawking’s overweening ambition and self-promotion, his repeated failure to acknowledge the work of others, his sexism and controlling behaviour were largely ignored because of his disability.”

Read the full review

The Newer World by Sebastian Barry

Reviewed by Sara Collins

Summed up in a sentence The memories of a formerly enslaved man in the aftermath of the American civil war.

What our reviewer said “I can think of no other writer who could describe blood and chaos in language that reaches for such a high register, and whose natural writerly empathy pre-empts the otherwise inevitable discussion about cultural appropriation.”

Read the full review

Taipei Story by Rebecca F Kuang

Reviewed by Kit Fan

Summed up in a sentence An American Chinese student attends a language school in Taiwan.

What our reviewer said “Kuang recreates the uncanny process of language acquisition, as if the reader is learning Mandarin side by side with Lily, sharing her joy and frustration.”

Read the full review

Further reading Rebecca F Kuang: ‘A Tale of Two Cities is deeply silly camp – I love it!’

Our Noble Selves by Kate Atkinson

Reviewed by Lucy Atkins

Summed up in a sentence A noirish mystery set around the 1951 Festival of Britain.

What our reviewer said “There is a gentle plea, here, for resilience and decency, couched in a nostalgia for a plucky and decent Britain that – if it ever existed – is certainly disappearing fast.”

Read the full review

The Castle by Jon Ronson

Reviewed by Anthony Cummins

Summed up in a sentence The journalist goes down the rabbit hole of modern masculinity.

What our reviewer said “Ronson makes these bizarre tales feel emblematic of topsy-turvy times, but you often sense an over-caffeinated logic at work.”

Read the full review

Further reading A party, 101 princesses and an eccentric millionaire: Jon Ronson on a mysterious castle – and what it taught him about masculinity in crisis

You may have missed …

The Vivisectors by Missouri Williams

Reviewed by Ian Maleney

Summed up in a sentence A cynical young woman navigates life, love and culture wars in this Booker-listed gothic saga set in a crumbling university town.

What our reviewer said “For all the layers of alienation and abjection which encrust Williams’s tale, there remains a model campus romance novel at its heart.”

Read the full review

If you only listen to one, make it …

Neil Young: Second Song

Reprise; available 18 September

Summed up in a sentence A late-period Neil Young album leaning into his gentle acoustic side, balancing intimations of mortality and occasional dashed-off moments with a beautiful 11-minute title track.

What our reviewer said “The sublime shares space with the not bad and the insubstantial: a superior example of a late-period Neil Young album, but a late-period Neil Young album nonetheless.” Alexis Petridis

Read the full review

Haruomi Hosono: Yours Sincerely

Ghostly International; out now

Summed up in a sentence Creative and captivating, the septuagenarian beloved by Harry Styles brings a hint of mischief to his innocently charming songs.

What our reviewer said “His 23rd solo album is wilful, playful, unpredictable and utterly beguiling. Rooted in the Japanese concept of omoiyari, roughly translated as compassion, these songs are big-hearted, focusing on warmth and positivity.” Stevie Chick

Read the full review

Gretchen Parlato: The Wise Ones

Summed up in a sentence With guests including Robert Glasper, Parlato turns her immaculate phrasing to soft funk, dancefloor numbers and interpretations of Stevie Wonder and Tears for Fears.

What our reviewer said “Perhaps aimed at a wider marketplace than its more improvisational and intimate predecessors Flor and Lean In, and not without a humdrum moment or two, The Wise Ones nonetheless confirms that Parlato’s inimitable character never lets her slip into the generic.” John Fordham

Read the full review

Lucas Debargue: Gershwin Variations

Summed up in a sentence Alongside supple and distinctive accounts of Rhapsody in Blue and the Piano Concerto and Preludes, the French pianist showcases his jazz chops in reinterpretations of Gershwin’s timeless songs.

What our reviewer said “His 12 virtuoso etudes on Gershwin songs, impeccable compositions in their own right, view familiar tunes through unfamiliar lenses. Embraceable You, for example, is reinvented as a sultry rumba, while Fascinating Rhythm is a cheeky Parisian waltz.” Clive Paget

Read the full review

Angine de Poitrine

Le Poisson Rouge, New York; touring now

Summed up in a sentence The brilliantly strange experimental band’s live show is a must-see spectacle powered by glorious noise and wild flair.

What our reviewer said “The songs had not especially changed from how they sound on their albums and in studios. The ability to finally see the duo’s superb musicianship up close carried the show – as did the reminders that they are still human.” Alexander Abnos

Read the full review

articles.title: The Guide #260: From Oasis to K-pop, music is going mad for the big-screen documentary
articles.text:
There’s a moment towards the end of Don’t Look Back in Anger, the newly released documentary capturing Oasis’s 2025 reunion tour, that helps explain why those planet-conquering gigs happened in the first place. Liam and Noel Gallagher are sitting down together for the rarest of paired interviews – the first since the 2009 scrap that broke up the band and created such a huge appetite for their return. Had Oasis’s story ended with that backstage fight in Paris, both Gallaghers note, their legacy would have been one of astonishing success curtailed by “chaos”. Instead, those reunion gigs, as well as proving wildly lucrative, have allowed them to add a triumphant coda to that messy ending. “It feels like a weight has been lifted,” a surprisingly contemplative Liam says.

That maybe makes Don’t Look Back in Anger sound more navel-gazing than this entertaining and often very funny film is – as you might expect of any doc that features a sweary rumination from Noel on Liam’s ability to balance a tambourine on his head (“If I did that I’d look an utter cunt, but somehow he does it and it’s the greatest thing I’ve ever seen”). Still, for all the droll quippery and bucket-hatted euphoria, there is something poignant and self-reflective at the film’s heart: hatchets are buried, departed friends are toasted and legacies are contemplated. What you leave behind was clearly on the minds of the brothers Gallagher throughout the tour and film.

And there’s no better way of shoring up your legacy, if you’re a musician or band tiptoeing toward heritage status, than having a documentary made about you. As last year’s record-breaking Becoming Led Zeppelin proved, these are platinum-status times for the music doc and its close cousin the concert film (Don’t Look Back in Anger, with its extensive use of archive footage, is a mix of both). Go to the cinema most weeks and there will be at least one screening – by my count there have been more than 30 this year alone, ranging from gleaming high-definition gigs by K-pop superstars you’ve only just heard of (Enhypen, Stray Kids, Ateez), to archive-rich career retrospectives of acts entering their autumn years (from Megadeth to James) and immaculate restorations of fuzzily remembered gigs from artists no longer with us (Soul to Soul, EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert). And that’s not including the many, many straight-to-streaming music docs and concert films, or scripted films – such as the box office-topping Michael Jackson biopic or the Green Day-authored coming-of-age comedy Nimrods – that serve the same reputation-burnishing purpose.

Ever since DA Pennebaker trained his camera on a Bob Dylan in 1967’s Don’t Look Back, the value of a well-made music doc has been obvious, but the current climate is particularly welcoming for the genre. Live footage has never been easier to capture or archive footage simpler to upload and digitise. And with the number of people going to the cinema still significantly down since the pandemic, there’s an enthusiasm among exhibitors to show films that lure in fandoms, particularly younger ones, that cinemas might otherwise not reach.

With studios and streamers lining up to take on these projects, artists, or artists’ estates, can demand a share of control over the finished product, particularly if they’re the ones with the rights to archive material and the songs themselves. (Though, intriguingly, Oasis don’t seem to have demanded editorial control over Don’t Look Back in Anger; had they done so, you imagine they might have nixed the extended footage of one fan wearing a kit of the Gallagher brothers’ hated Manchester United.)

Looking at the sea of concert films and music documentaries released in the last year, a generational divide of sorts jumps out between the former and the latter. Younger artists, without much of a history to trumpet, are largely the subjects of concert films, where the kineticism of their live shows can be shown off, enticing fans who didn’t catch the actual gig to start saving up for that next tour. Older artists with extensive archives and a long, winding narrative to draw from are more likely to be profiled in documentaries, or documentary-concert film hybrids, where they make their case for a place in pop’s pantheon.

Don’t Look Back in Anger goes further than many of its peers, though, by suggesting the band’s music has grown beyond their control, becoming part of some sort of wider folk memory. “You want to be writing songs that people take and stick into their lives and go ‘It’s mine now’,” Liam says, and the documentary goes out of its way to show that transference, spending as much time with Oasis fans, from Argentinian football ultras to Korean oyster-divers, as it does with the Gallaghers. Perhaps its most stirring moment comes during the gigs in Manchester’s Heaton Park, where instead of paid-up fans, the cameras follow those clambering over fences for a communal ticketless sing-along of Bring It on Down, as if the music has passed from possession of the band to the wider public.

That framing may sound self-aggrandising, but we are shown compelling evidence: just witness the footage of Don’t Look Back in Anger (the song) being spontaneously sung at the vigil for the 2017 Manchester Arena bombing. In another scene, a priest uses the Gallaghers’ reunion to highlight the importance of forgiveness – playing to the cameras, perhaps, but there’s a distinctly religious quality to some of the footage here: the ecstatic wailing of fans, the mass devotional sing-alongs.

Perhaps that’s the power of music – or a slickly produced documentary, at least: to make our ephemeral rock stars immortal.
